question: H1
answer:
REGULATORY DETERMINATION — MINIMUM REST BETWEEN DUTY PERIODS FOR US FLIGHT ATTENDANTS

ANSWER
=====
A US airline operating under 14 CFR Part 121 must give a flight attendant at least 10 consecutive hours of scheduled rest between the completion of one scheduled duty period and the commencement of the next. That 10-hour figure is a hard floor: 14 CFR 121.467(b)(3) states the rest period 'may not be reduced to less than 10 consecutive hours.'

Higher figures apply in two situations:
- 12 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is scheduled to a duty period of more than 14 but not more than 20 hours (121.467(b)(7)).
- 10 consecutive hours immediately before duty with at least 8 uninterrupted hours of sleep opportunity, plus 30 consecutive hours free from all duty in the past 168, if the certificate holder elects the Part 117 alternative under 121.467(c).

LEGAL BASIS
===========
Primary: 14 CFR 121.467(b) — 'Flight attendant duty period limitations and rest requirements: domestic, flag, and supplemental operations.' Applies to certificate holders conducting domestic, flag, or supplemental operations, i.e., scheduled and charter passenger airlines operating under Part 121. It does not reach Part 135 commuter/on-demand operators, which have no equivalent flight-attendant rest rule.

Definition of rest (121.467(a)): 'the period free of all restraint or duty for a certificate holder conducting domestic, flag, or supplemental operations and free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise.' Rest is measured from completion of the scheduled duty period to commencement of the subsequent duty period; it excludes deplaning/close-out duty at the front end and report time at the back end, both of which sit outside the rest window.

THE COMPLETE REST TABLE (current rule)
======================================
Situation | Minimum rest | Reducible? | Citation
Scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less | 10 consecutive hours | No — floor is absolute | 121.467(b)(2), (b)(3)
Scheduled duty period >14 hours and <=20 hours | 12 consecutive hours | Yes, to 10, but only if followed by a subsequent rest of >=14 consecutive hours that begins no later than 24 hours after the start of the reduced rest | 121.467(b)(7), (b)(8)
Cumulative relief | 24 consecutive hours free from all further duty during any 7 consecutive calendar days | No | 121.467(b)(13)
Part 117 election (optional carrier-wide) | 10 consecutive hours immediately before reserve or flight duty, measured from release from duty, providing >=8 uninterrupted hours of sleep opportunity; plus 30 consecutive hours free from all duty within the past 168 consecutive hours; plus 56 consecutive hours upon return to home base if the crew member travels more than 60 degrees of longitude and is away from home base more than 168 consecutive hours | 117.25(e), (b), (d); enabled by 121.467(c)

Note on the two 10-hour figures: under the default 121.467(b) regime, 10 hours is the irreducible floor for ordinary duty days. Under the (b)(8) reduced-rest option, 10 hours is a temporary concession that must be repaid with a 14-hour rest within 24 hours. Under the Part 117 election, 10 hours is the ordinary pre-duty rest and is measured from release from duty with an 8-hour sleep-opportunity content requirement. These are three different mechanisms that happen to share the number 10; a compliance check must identify which regime the carrier's operations specifications and manual prescribe.

WORKED EXAMPLES
================
1. Ordinary domestic turn. Duty period 11h30m, released 20:00 local. Rest = 10 consecutive hours, so earliest report is 06:00 the next day. The carrier may not schedule 09:00-to-19:00 duty followed by a 07:00 report (12 hours is fine; the point is that 10 is the number below which scheduling is prohibited, not a target).
2. Long duty day. Scheduled duty period 16h00m, released 22:00. Required rest = 12 consecutive hours; earliest report 10:00.
3. Reduced rest under (b)(8). Same 16-hour duty day; carrier elects to give only 10 hours (report 08:00). The reduced rest began at 22:00; the carrier must schedule the next rest period of at least 14 consecutive hours beginning no later than 22:00 the following day.
4. Seven-day relief. A flight attendant may be worked across a sequence of days but must receive 24 consecutive hours free from all duty within each rolling 7 consecutive calendar days.
5. Layover vs. home base. Under 121.467 the 10-hour (or 12-hour) minimum is identical at a layover station and at home base. Unlike Part 117 flightcrew rules, 121.467 contains no separate home-base rest (e.g., no 56-hour post-long-haul rule) unless the carrier has elected Part 117 under (b)/(c).

DISCREPANCY TO FLAG — SUPERSEDED GUIDANCE
=========================================
The FAA's public FAQ page ('What are the flight attendant duty period and rest requirements?') still displays the pre-amendment figures: 'at least nine consecutive hours of scheduled rest,' reducible 'under certain circumstances' to eight consecutive hours followed by a 10-hour rest. That reflects the earlier version of 121.467 and is not the current rule. The current eCFR text of 14 CFR 121.467(b)(2)-(3) requires 10 consecutive hours and prohibits reduction below 10. The rule was tightened following the 2018 FAA Reauthorization Act (Pub. L. 115-254, sec. 335), which directed the FAA to prescribe flight attendant duty and rest limits. Where the FAQ and the eCFR disagree, the eCFR controls. Anyone citing 'nine hours' or 'eight hours' as the current US minimum is quoting stale material.

SCOPE LIMITS AND CAVEATS
========================
1. This is the federal regulatory floor, not the operative number on any given trip. Collective bargaining agreements under the Railway Labor Act routinely set higher minimums (commonly 11-12 hours at layover, with hotel-quality and duty-time rigs). Contractual rest above the regulatory minimum is fully enforceable and is the number a flight attendant usually experiences.
2. State law does not raise this floor for Part 121 carriers; airline rates, routes, and services — including crew rest — are preempted by the Airline Deregulation Act, 49 U.S.C. 41713, and the FAA's field preemption over safety. Do not advise a carrier to look to state rest statutes for Part 121 flight attendants.
3. Domestic and international flying conducted by a US certificate holder is subject to the same federal minimum; foreign jurisdictions may impose their own rest rules on the ground at the layover station, and those can bind the schedule in practice.
4. Rest must be free of all restraint or duty. Being on call, being required to remain reachable, or being assigned ground duties during the window converts the period into duty and restarts the clock.
5. 121.467(b)(14) provides that a flight attendant is not considered scheduled in excess of duty limits where flights were scheduled and normally would terminate within the limits but circumstances beyond the carrier's control (e.g., weather) prevent timely arrival. This protects the carrier from a violation finding; it does not eliminate the rest obligation before the next duty period.
6. Compliance program: carriers must publish these limits in their operations/manuals, track scheduled rest against the 10/12-hour table, and document any (b)(8) reduced-rest pairing with its mandatory 14-hour follow-on within 24 hours. A carrier electing Part 117 under 121.467(c) must first establish written procedures as required by that paragraph.

BOTTOM LINE FOR THE ASK
=======================
10 consecutive hours is the answer for a US Part 121 airline between duty days. 12 consecutive hours applies when the duty period exceeded 14 hours (up to 20). Neither figure may be reduced below 10 consecutive hours, and any CBA the carrier has signed may require more.

TECHNICAL NOTE — Maximum weight for a 'small unmanned aircraft' (small drone) under U.S. FAA rules

1. ANSWER

A drone still counts as a 'small drone' (FAA term: small unmanned aircraft / sUAS) if it weighs LESS THAN 55 POUNDS on takeoff, including everything that is on board or otherwise attached to the aircraft.

- Numeric ceiling: 55 lb (pounds avoirdupois).
- The bound is EXCLUSIVE. 54.99 lb qualifies; exactly 55.00 lb does not.
- Metric equivalent: 55 lb = 24.94758035 kg. Safe working figure: less than 24.9476 kg.
- Weight basis: takeoff weight, all-up — airframe + battery/fuel + camera + gimbal + payload + cargo + any attached external load + attached accessories.

2. AUTHORITY AND EXACT REGULATORY TEXT

Primary source — 14 CFR § 107.3 (Definitions), Title 14, Chapter I, Subchapter F, Part 107, Subpart A (current eCFR text, as amended by Amdt. 107-8, 86 FR 4381, Jan. 15, 2021):

  "Small unmanned aircraft means an unmanned aircraft weighing less than 55 pounds on takeoff, including everything that is on board or otherwise attached to the aircraft."

Corroborating FAA sources:
- FAA, Summary of Small Unmanned Aircraft Rule (Part 107), June 21, 2016: "Unmanned aircraft must weigh less than 55 lbs. (25 kg)."
- FAA AC 107-2, § 4.2.6: "Small Unmanned Aircraft (UA). A UA weighing less than 55 pounds, including everything that is onboard or otherwise attached to the aircraft..."
- FAA AC 107-2, § 5.14.1 (transport of property): "The maximum total weight of the small UA (including any property being transported) is limited to under 55 pounds."
- FAA newsroom, Small UAS Regulations (Part 107): rules "cover ... drones weighing less than 55 pounds"; property-for-hire carriage allowed "provided the drone (including its attached systems), payload, and cargo, weighs less than 55 pounds total."
- FAA AIM, Chapter 11, Section 1: "part 107 operations are limited to small UAS (sUAS) weighing less than 55 pounds"; and "civil, non-recreational UAS weighing 55 pounds or more MGOW" operate under Part 91.

Statutory parallel (for cross-reference, not a substitute for the regulation): 49 U.S.C. § 44801 defines a small unmanned aircraft by the same under-55-pound takeoff-weight test.

3. WHAT COUNTS TOWARD THE 55 POUNDS

The regulation's phrase "including everything that is on board or otherwise attached to the aircraft" is the operative part. Counted at the moment of takeoff:
- Airframe, motors, propellers, landing gear
- Batteries or fuel (full takeoff load)
- Cameras, gimbals, sensors, lights, antennas, parachutes, transponders/Remote ID modules
- Any payload, package, cargo, or slung/external load
- Anything bolted, taped, zip-tied, or otherwise attached, and anything carried

Not counted: the ground-side control station / transmitter, the associated communication links and control components that are part of the UAS but not on the aircraft. Note the definitional split: "small unmanned aircraft" is the aircraft alone; "small unmanned aircraft system (small UAS)" is the aircraft plus its associated elements (§ 107.3). The 55 lb test applies to the aircraft, not the ground equipment.

Practical consequence: the weight test is continuous in practice — swapping to a larger battery, adding a payload, or fitting a heavier gimbal can push a compliant 52 lb aircraft over the line for that flight. Compliance is assessed per operation, at takeoff.

4. THE EDGE CASES THAT ACTUALLY BITE

(a) Strict inequality. 55.00 lb is outside the definition. If your scale reads 55.0 lb, you are not operating a small UAS. Build/plan to a margin (e.g., target ≤ 54.5 lb) so scale error and last-minute attachments don't put you over.

(b) The '25 kg' trap. The FAA summary prints "less than 55 lbs. (25 kg)." The metric figure is a rounding for convenience, and it rounds UP: 25.00 kg = 55.1156 lb, which is OVER the limit. If your drone's spec sheet says 25 kg, it does not qualify. Use the exact conversion: 55 lb = 24.9476 kg, so the metric ceiling is strictly less than 24.9476 kg (i.e., ≤ 24.94 kg to be safely inside).

(c) Category 1 is a different, much lower number. 14 CFR § 107.110(a)(1) sets Category 1 operations over people at 0.55 lb (≈0.2495 kg) or less on takeoff and throughout the operation. That is a sub-category of small UAS, not the small-UAS ceiling. Do not confuse 0.55 lb with 55 lb.

(d) Registration thresholds are also different. Recreational flyers must register aircraft over 0.55 lb (250 g); Part 107 operations require registration of the drone regardless of weight. Neither is the 'small drone' weight limit.

(e) Model aircraft wording differs slightly. Part 101 Subpart E / the statutory recreational exception describes model aircraft as "limited to not more than 55 pounds" unless certified through a community-based organization's design/construction/inspection/flight-test/safety program (see AC 107-2, Chapter 4). That is inclusive phrasing, in contrast to Part 107's "less than 55 pounds." If your operation is a pure § 44809 / Part 101 Subpart E model-aircraft operation, verify against that text; for anything under Part 107, the exclusive 55 lb ceiling in § 107.3 controls.

(f) The limit is not waivable. § 107.205 lists the regulations subject to waiver; the weight limit lives in the § 107.3 definition, so no Part 107 waiver can authorize a small UAS of 55 lb or more.

5. WHAT HAPPENS ABOVE 55 POUNDS

At 55 lb MGOW or more, the aircraft is not a small UAS and Part 107 is unavailable. Public UAS and civil non-recreational UAS at 55 lb or more MGOW operate under 14 CFR Part 91 (FAA AIM 11-1-x), which in practice means an experimental certificate under Part 21 (§ 21.191) and a Certificate of Waiver or Authorization (COA) for NAS access, with additional pilot and aircraft requirements. Type-certification pathways (Part 21) also become relevant. Weight also affects operations over people: Category 2 and Category 3 eligibility under Subpart D is keyed to kinetic energy and a declaration of compliance, but remains bounded by the small-UAS definition — a drone of 55 lb or more cannot use those categories at all.

6. QUICK REFERENCE TABLE (all values mutually consistent)

  Threshold | Value | Rule | Meaning
  Small UAS ceiling | < 55 lb (< 24.9476 kg) | 14 CFR 107.3 | Qualifies as a small unmanned aircraft
  Large UAS floor | ≥ 55 lb (≥ 24.9476 kg) | FAA AIM Ch. 11; Part 91 | Not a small UAS; Part 91/COA route
  Category 1 (over people) | ≤ 0.55 lb (≤ 0.2495 kg) | 14 CFR 107.110 | Lowest-risk sub-category; also no exposed lacerating rotating parts
  Recreational registration | > 0.55 lb (250 g) | 49 U.S.C. 44809; Part 48 | Registration trigger, not a size limit
  Part 107 registration | any weight | Part 107 / Part 48 | Every drone flown under Part 107 must be registered

  Conversion constants used: 1 lb = 0.45359237 kg; 55 lb = 24.94758035 kg; 0.55 lb = 0.2494758 kg; 25.00 kg = 55.1156 lb.

7. HOW TO STATE IT TO A STAKEHOLDER

"Under FAA rules a drone is a 'small unmanned aircraft' only if it weighs less than 55 pounds at takeoff, counting everything on board or attached — battery, camera, payload, cargo, and external loads. Fifty-five pounds exactly is over the line; the metric equivalent is under 24.9476 kg, and a drone spec'd at 25 kg does not qualify. Anything at or above 55 pounds falls outside Part 107 and must operate under Part 91 with an experimental certificate and a COA."

8. CURRENCY VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (do this before publishing or relying on the number)

Step 1. Open https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/subpart-A/section-107.3 and read the 'Small unmanned aircraft' definition. Confirm the string "weighing less than 55 pounds on takeoff, including everything that is on board or otherwise attached to the aircraft."
Step 2. If § 107.3 has been amended, record the amendment citation shown in the source note at the end of the section and update this note's citation line.
Step 3. Cross-check https://www.faa.gov/newsroom/small-unmanned-aircraft-systems-uas-regulations-part-107 for the plain-language figure and the cargo/payload sentence.
Step 4. Check the FAA AIM Chapter 11, Section 1 for the current large-UAS boundary wording ('MGOW 55 Pounds or More') so the two halves of the boundary still partition cleanly.
Step 5. If any source disagrees with 55 lb / 'less than', do not average or split the difference — treat the eCFR text as controlling and flag the discrepancy.

9. ASSUMPTIONS MADE (stated, not hidden)

- 'Small drone' means the FAA regulatory category 'small unmanned aircraft,' not a manufacturer or marketing classification.
- U.S. federal FAA rules apply; state/local rules are out of scope and cannot raise or lower this federal threshold.
- Current rules apply, not historical or proposed rulemaking.
- The question asks for the weight threshold only, not a full compliance analysis; the registration/Remote ID/over-people material above is included only to prevent the common threshold mix-ups.

# Basic VFR Weather Minimums — Class E Airspace Below 10,000 ft MSL

## Framework assumption (stated explicitly)
This answer is written to U.S. FAA rules, **14 CFR § 91.155** (Basic VFR weather minimums), as reproduced in **FAA AIM TBL 3-1-1**. If the operation is instead under ICAO Annex 2 or another State's rules, the numbers differ and must be looked up in that authority's table — the figures below do not transfer.

## The answer

| Item | Requirement (Class E, below 10,000 ft MSL) |
|---|---|
| Flight visibility | **3 statute miles** |
| Distance from clouds — below | **500 feet** |
| Distance from clouds — above | **1,000 feet** |
| Distance from clouds — horizontal | **2,000 feet** |

There is **no day/night difference** in Class E; the same minimums apply at all hours. Class E minimums are also identical to Class C and Class D minimums below 10,000 ft MSL — what distinguishes Class E is that no radio/endorsement or specific equipment is required, not the weather minimums.

## Regulatory text behind it
14 CFR 91.155(a), table row:

> Class E:
> Less than 10,000 feet MSL — 3 statute miles — 500 feet below. 1,000 feet above. 2,000 feet horizontal.
> At or above 10,000 feet MSL — 5 statute miles — 1,000 feet below. 1,000 feet above. 1 statute mile horizontal.

AIM 3-1-4 frames the rule: *"No person may operate an aircraft under basic VFR when the flight visibility is less, or at a distance from clouds that is less, than that prescribed for the corresponding altitude and class of airspace."*

## Boundary and interpretation notes (these matter in practice)
1. **"Below 10,000 ft MSL" is strict.** At exactly 10,000 ft MSL you are in the upper row: 5 statute miles visibility, 1,000 ft below / 1,000 ft above / **1 statute mile horizontal**. Climbing through 10,000 ft MSL requires the higher visibility and the much larger horizontal clearance.
2. **Cloud distances are clearance distances, not minimums to be rounded down.** 500 ft below / 1,000 ft above / 2,000 ft horizontal is the minimum; any margin is the pilot's own.
3. **MSL vs. AGL.** The Class E row is indexed by MSL altitude, unlike Class G, which is indexed by height above the surface. Class E airspace extending to the surface (e.g., a Class E surface area at an airport) still uses the same "less than 10,000 ft MSL" row — but paragraphs (c) and (d) of § 91.155 then apply (see below).
4. **Class E base-altitude rule — § 91.155(e):** *"an aircraft operating at the base altitude of a Class E airspace area is considered to be within the airspace directly below that area."* So at the base of a Class E layer you use the Class E (or Class G) minimums of the airspace below, not those above.
5. **Surface-area additional restrictions — § 91.155(c) and (d):** inside the lateral boundaries of controlled airspace designated to the surface for an airport, no VFR flight below the ceiling when the ceiling is less than 1,000 ft; and no takeoff, landing or traffic-pattern entry unless ground visibility is at least 3 statute miles (or, where ground visibility is not reported, flight visibility at least 3 statute miles). Special VFR (§ 91.157) is the relief valve for both.
6. **More-restrictive-airspace rule (AIM 3-1-3):** where Class E overlaps Class B/C/D, the more restrictive airspace's rules apply. Conversely, Class E is more restrictive than Class G — so do not substitute the Class G 1-statute-mile / clear-of-clouds day minimums when the airspace is in fact Class E.
7. **Do not confuse this row with Class G.** Class G below 1,200 ft AGL (day, non-helicopter) is 1 statute mile and clear of clouds; that is a different airspace class and a different row.

## One-line answer for operational use
In Class E below 10,000 ft MSL: **3 statute miles flight visibility; remain 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 2,000 ft horizontally from clouds — day or night.**

## Units and verification
Visibility in **statute miles** (U.S. domestic), cloud clearances in **feet**. Source: 14 CFR § 91.155(a) table; FAA AIM 3-1-4, TBL 3-1-1; corroborated by the 2016 CFR print edition of § 91.155.

# OSHA Exposure Limits for Respirable Crystalline Silica — General Industry

## 1. The two values

| Limit | Value | Averaging basis | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Permissible exposure limit (PEL)** | **50 µg/m³** (0.050 mg/m³) | 8-hour time-weighted average (TWA) | 29 CFR 1910.1053(c) |
| **Action level (AL)** | **25 µg/m³** (0.025 mg/m³) | 8-hour TWA | 29 CFR 1910.1053(b), definition of "Action level" |

Regulatory text, PEL — 1910.1053(c): "The employer shall ensure that no employee is exposed to an airborne concentration of respirable crystalline silica in excess of 50 µg/m3, calculated as an 8-hour TWA."

Regulatory text, action level — 1910.1053(b): "Action level means a concentration of airborne respirable crystalline silica of 25 µg/m3, calculated as an 8-hour TWA."

Both figures are 8-hour time-weighted averages of the **respirable** fraction only; they are not total dust and not a ceiling or short-term limit. The standard contains no separate STEL for silica.

## 2. Scope — which standard these numbers belong to

These are the **general industry** limits under **29 CFR 1910.1053** ("Respirable crystalline silica"), promulgated 2016 and in force as currently codified. The same section applies to general industry and to maritime (shipyard) employment; OSHA administers it as one standard for both.

Do **not** substitute the construction standard, **29 CFR 1926.1153**, which is a separate rule with its own Table 1 compliance option. (Its numeric limits happen to be the same — 50 µg/m³ PEL / 25 µg/m³ AL as 8-hour TWA — but the citation and the compliance mechanics differ, so cite the correct part for the industry in question.)

## 3. What each threshold triggers

- **Below 25 µg/m³ (below the action level):** the exposure-assessment, medical-surveillance, and (with exceptions) written-program duties are not triggered. Note also 1910.1053(a)(2): the section does not apply at all where the employer has **objective data** demonstrating that employee exposure will remain **below 25 µg/m³ as an 8-hour TWA** under any foreseeable conditions. That exemption threshold is numerically identical to the action level — this is intentional and is not a discrepancy.
- **At or above 25 µg/m³ (at/above the action level):** exposure assessment is required under 1910.1053(d)(1); repeat monitoring at least every 6 months while exposures remain at or above the AL but at or below the PEL [1910.1053(d)(3)(iii)]; medical surveillance must be offered under 1910.1053(i) to employees exposed at or above the AL for 30 or more days per year.
- **Above 50 µg/m³ (above the PEL):** overexposure — engineering and work-practice controls, respiratory protection, and repeat monitoring within 3 months [1910.1053(d)(3)(iv)] apply.
- **Below 25 µg/m³ on non-initial monitoring:** monitoring may be discontinued only after two consecutive measurements taken 7 or more days apart are below the AL [1910.1053(d)(3)(v)].

## 4. Definitions needed to apply the numbers

- **Respirable crystalline silica** (1910.1053(b)): "quartz, cristobalite, and/or tridymite contained in airborne particles that are determined to be respirable by a sampling device designed to meet the characteristics for respirable-particle-size-selective samplers specified in ISO 7708:1995." The limit therefore applies to the ISO/CEN-consistent respirable size fraction, not to total airborne dust.
- **This section** (1910.1053(b)): the respirable crystalline silica standard, 29 CFR 1910.1053.

## 5. How compliance is determined against these numbers

1. Collect a personal breathing-zone sample with a cyclone/selector meeting the ISO 7708:1995 respirable convention (e.g., 10 mm nylon cyclone at 1.7 L/min, or the GK2.69 at 4.2 L/min), full-shift where feasible.
2. Analyze by a validated method for crystalline silica — OSHA ID-142 (by XRD or IR) or NIOSH 7500/7602 — reporting quartz, cristobalite and tridymite.
3. Compute the 8-hour TWA: TWA = Σ(Cᵢ·Tᵢ) / 8, where Cᵢ is the concentration in each sampled period (µg/m³) and Tᵢ its duration in hours (sample results for periods over 8 hours are capped at 8 h in the standard calculation).
4. Compare: TWA ≥ 25 µg/m³ → action level met/exceeded; TWA > 50 µg/m³ → PEL exceeded. Because the two limits are exactly a factor of two apart, any computed TWA between 25 and 50 µg/m³ is a valid "at or above AL, at or below PEL" result — a figure in that band does not violate either limit.

## 6. Cautions when quoting these numbers

- **Do not conflate with other limits.** The ACGIH TLV-TWA for quartz is 0.025 mg/m³ (25 µg/m³) — numerically equal to OSHA's action level but a different instrument with different legal effect. OSHA's pre-2016 general-industry limits (the quartz formula and the million-particles-per-cubic-foot limits in the older 1910.1000 tables) are superseded for respirable crystalline silica by 1910.1053 and must not be cited as the current PEL.
- **State-plan states** may enforce an identical or stricter limit; the federal figures above are the floor.
- **Version currency.** The figures above are as currently codified in 29 CFR 1910.1053 on eCFR; no amendment has changed the 50/25 µg/m³ values since the 2016 rule. If a specific edition or date of citation is required, cite "29 CFR 1910.1053(c) and (b), as currently in force."

## Answer

For **CVE-2021-44228** (Log4Shell), the US National Vulnerability Database (NVD) assigns:

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| CVSS version | 3.1 |
| Base score | **10.0** |
| Qualitative severity | **Critical** |
| Vector string | `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H` |

## Evidence

Two independent sources reproduce NVD's value and vector:

1. **AWS ALAS CVE page** — the 'CVSS Scores' table contains a row explicitly labelled `NVD` / `CVSSv3` with score `10.0` and vector `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H`.
2. **Red Hat CVE page** — the 'CVSS v3 Score Breakdown' table lists `NVD` Base Score `10`, with Scope `Changed`, and the remaining metrics `AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/C:H/I:H/A:H`.

The canonical NVD record is:

`https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2021-44228`

## Verification by CVSS v3.1 calculation

Using the NVD vector `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H`:

- Impact subscores: C:H = 0.56, I:H = 0.56, A:H = 0.56
- ISS = 1 - (1 - 0.56)^3 = 0.914816
- Scope is Changed, so:
  - Impact = 7.52 x (ISS - 0.029) - 3.25 x (ISS - 0.02)^15
  - Impact = 7.52 x 0.885816 - 3.25 x (0.894816)^15
  - Impact ≈ 6.6613 - 0.6136 ≈ 6.0477
- Exploitability = 8.22 x AV(0.85) x AC(0.77) x PR(0.85) x UI(0.85)
  - Exploitability ≈ 3.8870
- Base = Roundup(min(1.08 x (Impact + Exploitability), 10))
  - 1.08 x (6.0477 + 3.8870) ≈ 10.73, capped at 10
  - Base score = **10.0**

## Important distinction

NVD's score is **10.0** with **Scope Changed**. Red Hat publishes a different vendor-specific score of **9.8** with **Scope Unchanged**; that is not NVD's score and should not be substituted for it. NVD's CVSS v2 score of 9.3 is also irrelevant to this request, which asks specifically for CVSS v3.1.

## Severity mapping

Under the CVSS v3.1 qualitative severity scale, a base score of 10.0 falls in the **Critical** range (9.0-10.0). NVD therefore rates CVE-2021-44228 as **Critical** with a CVSS v3.1 base score of **10.0**.

The 1876 first edition of Robert's Rules of Order (the Pocket Manual carried by Project Gutenberg as e-text #9097) requires a TWO-THIRDS VOTE to adopt — i.e., to order — a motion for the Previous Question. A simple majority is not sufficient; the motion fails unless two-thirds of the votes cast are in the affirmative.

1. SCOPE AND SENSE OF THE QUESTION

- Source: the 1876 first edition only, as transcribed at Project Gutenberg #9097 (https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/9097; plain text at https://www.gutenberg.org/files/9097/9097-0.txt). No later edition (1893 revised, 1915 4th, 1951 10th, 2011 11th) is used to supply or override the value.
- 'Adopt' = the passage of the Previous Question motion itself, i.e., the vote by which the assembly agrees to put the pending (main) question to an immediate vote. It is NOT the vote subsequently taken on the main question; once the Previous Question is ordered, the main question is disposed of by whatever vote that question independently requires (ordinarily a majority; two-thirds for, e.g., a proposal to amend a constitution or bylaws).
- The manual's phrasing for the threshold is the standard one: the Previous Question 'requires a two-thirds vote.'

2. WHERE THE 1876 MANUAL STATES IT

- Governing passage: Article VI, 'Previous Question' (opening section, §20 in the ordinary numbering of the 1876 printing). This is the article that defines the motion, states its form ('Shall the main question be now put?'), states that it is undebatable, and fixes its vote requirement at two-thirds.
- Corroboration A: the 'Table of Rules Relating to Motions' printed at the back of Part I, whose vote column records 2/3 against the Previous Question (in printings that carry that column).
- Corroboration B: the Previous Question is grouped in the manual with the other motions that require more than a majority (suspension of the rules; taking up a question out of its proper order; making a special order).
- Reconciling multiple statements: there is no conflict to resolve — every place the 1876 text speaks to the point gives two-thirds. The priority rule, if a printing ever appeared to conflict, is that the definitional article (Art. VI) governs over a summary table, and a summary table governs over nothing else.

3. BASE OF THE TWO-THIRDS

A two-thirds vote means two-thirds of the votes cast (the manual's general definition of a two-thirds vote), not two-thirds of the membership and not two-thirds of those present who abstain. Consequences: a tie fails; 66 of 100 cast fails; 67 of 100 cast carries.

question: H13
answer:
# Luminous efficacy Kcd in the SI Brochure, 9th edition (2019)

## 1. The fixed value (ask 1)

**Kcd = 683 lm/W**, exactly — no uncertainty, infinite significant figures.

Wording of the 9th edition, list of the seven defining constants on which the SI is based:

> "• the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10^12 Hz, Kcd, is 683 lm/W,"

The same value appears in Table 1 (the seven base units), in the definition of the candela:

> "The candela, symbol cd, is the SI unit of luminous intensity in a given direction. It is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10^12 Hz, Kcd, to be 683 when expressed in the unit lm W^−1, which is equal to cd sr W^−1, or cd sr kg^−1 m^−2 s^3, where the kilogram, metre and second are defined in terms of h, c and ΔνCs."

Note the two equivalent phrasings and use the right one for the context: the *numerical value* is 683 when Kcd is expressed in lm W^−1 (this is the form used in the defining text of the candela); the *constant itself* is 683 lm/W (this is the form used in the list of defining constants). Both are the same statement.

Unit equivalences given by the Brochure: lm = cd sr, W = kg m^2 s^−3, hence lm W^−1 = cd sr W^−1 = cd sr kg^−1 m^−2 s^3.

Exactness: the Brochure states that "These definitions specify the exact numerical value of each constant when its value is expressed in the corresponding SI unit." So 683 lm/W is a fixed, exact defining value — it is not a measured quantity and carries no uncertainty and no trailing "approximately". It should never be written as 683.00 or with a ± term, and it should not be rounded to "about 683".

## 2. The frequency (ask 2)

**ν = 540 × 10^12 Hz = 540 THz = 5.4 × 10^14 Hz**, exactly (the frequency is a specified integer multiple of the hertz, fixed by the definition, not a measured wavelength).

The definition is given *by frequency*, not by wavelength. This is deliberate: a frequency is independent of the medium, whereas the corresponding wavelength depends on the refractive index of the medium.

## 3. The wavelength that corresponds to it — stated correctly

Appendix 2 to the 9th edition ("SI Brochure – 9th edition (2019) – Appendix 2", v1.02, 22 March 2021), §3.1, gives the equivalent wavelength in standard air:

> "where λa = 555.017 nm is the wavelength in standard air at the frequency of 540 × 10^12 Hz given in the definition of Kcd"

So:
- The defining quantity is **540 × 10^12 Hz**.
- The commonly quoted "555 nm" is a rounded, in-air equivalent of that frequency; the Brochure's own figure is **555.017 nm in standard air**.
- In vacuum the equivalent wavelength is c/ν = 299 792 458 / (540 × 10^12) m ≈ 555.171 nm.
- None of these wavelengths is part of the definition; do not present any of them as the defining condition.

## 4. Scope and status of the value

- The definition is for monochromatic radiation at that one frequency only. For any other source, Appendix 2 §3.1 defines photometric quantities by weighting the spectral power distribution with the CIE spectral luminous efficiency function V(λ) and converting to absolute photometric values using Kcd:
  Xv = Kcd ∫ Xe,λ(λ) V(λ) dλ.
- Kcd is one of the seven defining constants of the revised SI that took effect on 20 May 2019; it links the photometric units to the corresponding radiometric units and is the basis of the candela definition. It is not derived from, and does not depend on, any artefact or material property (the old 540 × 10^12 Hz / 555 nm platinum-freezing-point formulation is superseded).
- The same wording and the same two numbers (683; 540 × 10^12 Hz) appear verbatim in the 9th edition's Appendix 2 (v1.02, 22 March 2021), so the answer is stable across the 9th edition and its reprints/appendices.

## 5. Direct answer, in one sentence

In the SI Brochure, 9th edition (2019), the fixed numerical value of the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency **540 × 10^12 Hz (540 THz)** is **Kcd = 683 lm/W** (683 when expressed in the unit lm W^−1 = cd sr W^−1 = cd sr kg^−1 m^−2 s^3), exactly.

question: H15
answer:
CLASSIFICATION DETERMINATION — Liquid, closed-cup flash point 65 °C, no other hazard class; US domestic transport (49 CFR Parts 171–180)

1. ANSWER

No. A liquid with a flash point of 65 °C is not a Class 3 flammable liquid under 49 CFR 173.120(a). It is a COMBUSTIBLE LIQUID as defined in 49 CFR 173.120(b)(1) (flash point above 60 °C and below 93 °C, and does not meet the definition of any other hazard class). "Combustible liquid" is a DOT definition, not one of the nine hazard classes. For domestic transportation in non-bulk packagings it is not regulated as a hazardous material under the HMR; when offered in bulk packagings it is subject to the HMR's combustible-liquid provisions.

2. GOVERNING TEXT (49 CFR 173.120, as retrieved from the 2023, 2024 and 2025 CFR editions and eCFR; all four are consistent on the thresholds)

173.120(a) Flammable liquid: "a flammable liquid (Class 3) means a liquid having a flash point of not more than 60 °C (140 °F), or any material in a liquid phase with a flash point at or above 37.8 °C (100 °F) that is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging, with the following exceptions: (1) Any liquid meeting one of the definitions specified in §173.115. (2) Any mixture having one or more components with a flash point of 60 °C (140 °F) or higher, that make up at least 99 percent of the total volume of the mixture, if the mixture is not offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point. (3) Any liquid with a flash point greater than 35 °C (95 °F) that does not sustain combustion according to ASTM D 4206 ... or the procedure in appendix H of this part. (4) Any liquid with a flash point greater than 35 °C (95 °F) and with a fire point greater than 100 °C (212 °F) according to ISO 2592 ..."

173.120(b)(1) Combustible liquid: "any liquid that does not meet the definition of any other hazard class specified in this subchapter and has a flash point above 60 °C (140 °F) and below 93 °C (200 °F)."

173.120(b)(2): a flammable liquid with a flash point at or above 38 °C (100 °F) that meets no other hazard class may be reclassed as a combustible liquid (not available for vessel/air except where other means is impracticable); an elevated-temperature material that is Class 3 because it is intentionally heated may not be so reclassed.

173.120(b)(3): a combustible liquid that does not sustain combustion (ASTM D 4206 or appendix H procedure) is not subject to the subchapter as a combustible liquid.

173.120(c)(1): the flash point must be determined by a closed-cup method — ASTM D 56, D 3278 or D 3828 for a homogeneous, single-phase liquid with viscosity below 45 S.U.S. at 38 °C that does not form a surface film; otherwise ASTM D 93, D 3278, or ISO 1516/1523/2719/3679/3680/13736. 173.120(c)(2): for a mixture of compounds of differing volatility, the flash point is determined on the material in the form in which it is to be shipped.

3. STEP-BY-STEP DETERMINATION

Prong 1 — flash point not more than 60 °C:
  Measured value 65 °C. Test: is 65 ≤ 60? No. Prong 1 fails.

Prong 2 — elevated-temperature material in a bulk packaging:
  Requires ALL of: (i) flash point at or above 37.8 °C — satisfied (65 ≥ 37.8); (ii) intentionally heated; (iii) offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point; (iv) in a bulk packaging. On the stated facts the material is not intentionally heated and bulk status is not asserted, so (ii)–(iv) are not met. Prong 2 fails. (See §4 for the case where it does not.)

Exceptions 173.120(a)(1)–(a)(5):
  These only remove a material from Class 3; they cannot create Class 3 status and are not reached because the material already fails both prongs.

Result: not a Class 3 flammable liquid. Not a hazardous material by any Class 3 route.

Combustible-liquid test, 173.120(b)(1):
  "Does not meet the definition of any other hazard class" — given by the request. "Flash point above 60 °C and below 93 °C" — 65 > 60 and 65 < 93. Satisfied. Classification: COMBUSTIBLE LIQUID, 49 CFR 173.120(b)(1).

Packing group / hazard zone: not assigned. PG assignment and hazard zones (173.121) apply to Class 3 materials; this is not one.

4. WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE ANSWER (sensitivity of the verdict)

(a) Elevated temperature in bulk. If the material is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above 65 °C in a bulk packaging, it becomes Class 3 by the second prong of 173.120(a) even though its flash point is 65 °C. It then cannot be reclassed as a combustible liquid (173.120(b)(2), final sentence). Confirm the shipping temperature and packaging capacity before finalizing.

(b) Test-method validity. The 60 °C cut is a closed-cup criterion. If the 65 °C figure came from an open-cup method (e.g., Cleveland open cup ASTM D 92 or a Tag open cup), it is not a valid basis for classification; open-cup results typically read higher than closed-cup, so the true closed-cup value could fall at or below 60 °C and the material would be Class 3. Confirm the reported result was obtained by a 173.120(c)(1) method, and that the method matches the liquid's viscosity/surface-film behavior (D 56 only for low-viscosity, non-film-forming liquids; otherwise D 93 or an equivalent listed method).

(c) Mixtures. For a mixture of components of differing volatility, 173.120(c)(2) requires the flash point to be run on the material as shipped, with a second test under the conditions that paragraph specifies. A supplier's literature value for a nominal composition is not a substitute.

(d) Measurement margin. The reported 65 °C sits only 5 °C above the 60 °C threshold. Check the reported result against the precision statement of the method actually used and, if the result's uncertainty band straddles 60 °C, obtain replicate results before committing to a non-Class 3 classification. The regulatory cut is strict ("not more than 60 °C"), so a result at 60 °C or below is Class 3.

(e) Sustained combustion. If the material is later shipped in bulk as a combustible liquid, run ASTM D 4206 or appendix H; a combustible liquid that does not sustain combustion is not subject to the subchapter as a combustible liquid (173.120(b)(3)).

5. REGULATORY CONSEQUENCES

Non-bulk, domestic: not regulated as a hazardous material under the HMR — no HMT entry, shipping paper, package marking/labeling, placarding, or UN packaging requirement arises from Part 173. Note that §173.150(f) ("Exceptions for Class 3 (flammable) and combustible liquids") is the operative exception for combustible liquids in non-bulk packagings; read the current text of that paragraph to confirm its exact scope and any residual requirements before finalizing documentation.

Bulk, domestic: regulated as a combustible liquid. The domestic Hazardous Materials Table entry normally used when a specific proper shipping name does not apply is NA1993, "Combustible liquid, n.o.s." Read the class, label, special-provision, packaging and quantity-limit columns of the current 172.101 HMT for that entry, and apply Part 172 subparts C and E and the applicable bulk packaging requirements in Part 173. Confirm placarding treatment for bulk combustible liquids against 172.504 before shipping.

Vessel/air: outside the stated scope. Note that the 173.120(b)(2) reclass mechanism is unavailable for vessel/air except where other means of transportation is impracticable; separately, the international modal rules (IMDG Code, ICAO/IATA) also use a 60 °C closed-cup cut for Class 3, so this material would not be Class 3 there either — but re-verify if any leg moves by vessel or aircraft.

6. NUMERIC CROSS-CHECK (all values used above)

65 °C (given) vs 60 °C (173.120(a) Class 3 upper bound): 65 > 60 — above the bound; not Class 3. Correct direction.
65 °C vs 93 °C (173.120(b)(1) combustible-liquid upper bound): 65 < 93 — inside the band. Consistent with the combustible-liquid conclusion.
65 °C vs 37.8 °C (173.120(a) elevated-temperature lower bound): 65 ≥ 37.8 — the elevated-temperature prong is live as a conditional, not as the answer.
60 °C = 140 °F; 93 °C = 199.4 °F (≈200 °F); 37.8 °C = 100 °F; 65 °C = 149 °F. All conversions consistent with the CFR's dual-unit thresholds.
No value in this determination violates a threshold it also states.

7. RECORDS TO HOLD AND VERIFICATION CHECKLIST

- Flash point test report: method (D 56 / D 93 / D 3278 / D 3828 / ISO method), closed-cup confirmation, sample identification, date, laboratory, and the as-shipped form of the material.
- Viscosity at 38 °C and surface-film observation, to justify the method selection under 173.120(c)(1)(i) vs (ii).
- Composition/mixture data supporting the "no other hazard class" premise (and, for mixtures, the 173.120(a)(2) 99-percent check).
- Shipping temperature and packaging capacity (bulk vs non-bulk) for the specific shipment — this is the only fact that can convert the answer to Class 3.
- Current-edition text of 173.120, 173.150(f), 172.101 (NA1993) and 172.504 at the time of shipment; the HMR is amended frequently.

8. NON-DOT REGIMES (outside the question, flagged so the classification is not misused)

OSHA 29 CFR 1910.106 / NFPA 30: a 65 °C (149 °F) flash point falls in Class IIIA (≥140 °F and <200 °F) — a combustible liquid for fire-code and storage purposes even though DOT does not regulate it in non-bulk. Environmental/SPCC and state fire-code obligations may also attach. These do not affect the DOT answer above.

question: H17
answer:
NRC PUBLIC DOSE LIMITS — 10 CFR PART 20, SUBPART D

GOVERNING PROVISION: 10 CFR 20.1301, 'Dose limits for individual members of the public' (Subpart D — Radiation Dose Limits for Individual Members of the Public; source 56 FR 23398, May 21, 1991, as amended at 60 FR 48625, 62 FR 4133, 67 FR 20370, 67 FR 62872). Text verified against the eCFR current edition (10 CFR 20.1301 and 20.1003; fetched 2026-11-17).

1. THE TWO LIMITS

| Limit | Regulatory citation | Value (traditional) | Value (SI) | Dose quantity / scope |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Annual, individual member of the public | 20.1301(a)(1) | 0.1 rem in a year (= 100 mrem) | 1 mSv in a year | Total Effective Dose Equivalent (TEDE) from the licensed operation — external + internal combined |
| Any one hour, unrestricted area | 20.1301(a)(2) | 0.002 rem in any one hour (= 2 mrem) | 0.02 mSv in any one hour (= 20 µSv) | Dose from EXTERNAL SOURCES only, in an unrestricted area |

Verbatim (20.1301(a)): 'Each licensee shall conduct operations so that— (1) The total effective dose equivalent to individual members of the public from the licensed operation does not exceed 0.1 rem (1 mSv) in a year, exclusive of the dose contributions from background radiation, from any medical administration the individual has received, from exposure to individuals administered radioactive material and released under § 35.75, from voluntary participation in medical research programs, and from the licensee's disposal of radioactive material into sanitary sewerage in accordance with § 20.2003, and (2) The dose in any unrestricted area from external sources, exclusive of the dose contributions from patients administered radioactive material and released in accordance with § 35.75, does not exceed 0.002 rem (0.02 millisievert) in any one hour.'

Note the structural asymmetry, which is the single most common source of error: the annual limit is a TEDE limit (internal intake dose included via committed effective dose equivalent), while the one-hour limit is an external-source limit only. There is no one-hour internal-dose limit; internal dose from effluents is controlled by the annual TEDE limit and by the effluent concentration limits of Appendix B, Table 2, as invoked in 20.1302(b)(2)(i).

2. DEFINITIONS THAT CONTROL APPLICABILITY (10 CFR 20.1003)

- Total Effective Dose Equivalent (TEDE): 'the sum of the effective dose equivalent (for external exposures) and the committed effective dose equivalent (for internal exposures).' This, not deep-dose equivalent or lens dose equivalent, is the quantity the annual public limit is written against.
- Member of the public: 'any individual except when that individual is receiving an occupational dose.' A declared pregnant worker, a monitored radiation worker, and anyone else in an occupational dose status is outside this definition while so exposed; patients and research subjects are handled instead through the explicit exclusions in (a)(1).
- Unrestricted area: 'an area, access to which is neither limited nor controlled by the licensee.' This is the geographic trigger for the 0.002 rem/h limit. It is defined by access control, not by ownership, fencing, or distance.
- Controlled area: 'an area, outside of a restricted area but inside the site boundary, access to which can be limited by the licensee for any reason.' Under 20.1301(b): 'If the licensee permits members of the public to have access to controlled areas, the limits for members of the public continue to apply to those individuals.' So the annual public limit follows the person into controlled areas the public may enter; the hourly external limit is textually tied to unrestricted areas.
- Dose limits: 'the permissible upper bounds of radiation doses.'

3. EXCLUSIONS BUILT INTO THE ANNUAL LIMIT (20.1301(a)(1))
Dose from the following is not counted toward the 0.1 rem (1 mSv) annual figure: (i) background radiation; (ii) any medical administration the individual has received; (iii) exposure to individuals administered radioactive material and released under 10 CFR 35.75; (iv) voluntary participation in medical research programs; (v) the licensee's disposal of radioactive material into sanitary sewerage under 10 CFR 20.2003. The one-hour limit (a)(2) carries a narrower exclusion: only dose contributions from § 35.75-released patients.

4. QUALIFICATIONS, ALTERNATIVES AND OVERLAYS
- Visitors to a patient who cannot be released under § 35.75: 20.1301(c) permits a dose above 0.1 rem (1 mSv) provided it does not exceed 0.5 rem (5 mSv) and the authorized user determined beforehand that the visit is appropriate. This is a conditional exception, not a public limit.
- NRC-authorized higher annual limit: 20.1301(d) allows a licensee or applicant to apply for prior NRC authorization to operate up to 0.5 rem (5 mSv) per year for an individual member of the public, supported by (1) need and expected duration, (2) a dose assessment and control program, and (3) procedures to keep dose ALARA. Absent a granted authorization, 0.1 rem (1 mSv) governs.
- EPA standards: 20.1301(e) requires licensees subject to 40 CFR Part 190 (environmental radiation standards for the uranium fuel cycle) to comply with those standards in addition. Those standards (e.g., 25 mrem/yr TEDE to any member of the public from the fuel-cycle facility) are separate and do not replace 20.1301.
- Additional restrictions: 20.1301(f) allows the Commission to impose further limits on radiation levels in unrestricted areas and on effluent quantities to restrict collective dose.
- ALARA: 10 CFR 20.1103 requires licensees subject to the effluent-ALARA provisions to achieve public dose as low as reasonably achievable, cost-beneficial; compliance with 0.1 rem/1 mSv is a ceiling, not a target.

5. HOW COMPLIANCE IS SHOWN (20.1302) — AND THE 0.05 rem/yr TRAP
20.1302(a) requires surveys of radiation levels in unrestricted and controlled areas and of radioactive materials in effluents. 20.1302(b) offers two routes:
 (b)(1) Demonstrate by measurement or calculation that the TEDE to the individual likely to receive the highest dose from the licensed operation does not exceed the annual limit; or
 (b)(2) Demonstrate that (i) annual average effluent concentrations at the unrestricted-area boundary do not exceed Appendix B, Table 2 values, and (ii) if an individual were continuously present in an unrestricted area, the dose from external sources would not exceed 0.002 rem (0.02 mSv) in an hour AND 0.05 rem (0.5 mSv) in a year.
CRITICAL DISTINCTION: the 0.05 rem (0.5 mSv) per year in 20.1302(b)(2)(ii) is a screening value used only in the (b)(2) alternative-compliance path, and it covers external sources only. It is NOT the public dose limit. The limit is 0.1 rem (1 mSv) TEDE per year under 20.1301(a)(1). A compliance case built on (b)(2)(ii) is more restrictive on the external pathway than the limit itself, which is why the two numbers coexist without conflict.

6. WHY THE HOURLY AND ANNUAL LIMITS DO NOT CONTRADICT EACH OTHER
0.002 rem/h sustained for a full year (8766 h) would total 17.532 rem (175.3 mSv) — roughly 175 times the annual limit. The hourly limit is therefore not a permissible sustained rate; it is a short-term ceiling that constrains transient or localized external radiation fields (e.g., a temporarily exposed source, a storage location, a point near a shielded boundary) in areas where members of the public may be present. Sustained occupancy is bounded by the annual TEDE limit, and the 20.1302(b)(2)(ii) 0.05 rem/yr external screening value corresponds to an average of about 5.7×10^-6 rem/h (0.057 µSv/h) over a year. Applying the 0.002 rem/h value as if it were an annual-rate allowance is the second most common error after confusing TEDE with external dose.

7. CONTRAST SET — VALUES THAT ARE NOT THE ANSWER (listed to prevent substitution)
- Occupational limits, 10 CFR 20.1201 (adults): 5 rem (50 mSv)/yr TEDE; 50 rem (0.5 Sv) shallow-dose equivalent to skin/extremities; 15 rem (0.15 Sv) lens dose equivalent. Minors: 10% of these (20.1207). Declared pregnant worker: 0.5 rem (5 mSv) to the embryo/fetus (20.1208). None of these apply to members of the public.
- 10 CFR 50, Appendix I design objectives for light-water reactors: 5 mrem/yr (0.05 mSv) TEDE from liquid effluents and 5 mrem/yr from gaseous effluents (with a 3 mrem/yr gamma and 5 mrem/yr beta dose-rate objective at the site boundary). Design objectives, not public dose limits.
- 40 CFR 61 Subpart I (NESHAP, radionuclide emissions): 10 mrem/yr ED (0.1 mSv) to any member of the public. A separate EPA program.
- 40 CFR 190 (uranium fuel cycle): 25 mrem/yr TEDE (0.25 mSv). Separate EPA program, applied cumulatively with 20.1301 via 20.1301(e).

8. UNITS AND REPORTING PRECISION
State both systems, as the regulation does: 0.1 rem (1 mSv) per year; 0.002 rem (0.02 mSv, i.e., 2 mrem or 20 µSv) in any one hour. Useful equivalents: 0.1 rem = 100 mrem = 1 mSv; 0.002 rem = 2 mrem = 0.02 mSv = 20 µSv. Report to the precision of the rule text (one significant figure for the annual value, one for the hourly value in rem); do not round 0.002 rem to 0.0020 or to 2 mrem/h in a way that loses the regulatory figure.

9. DIRECT ANSWERS
- Per year, individual member of the public, from a licensee's operations: 0.1 rem (1 mSv) TEDE, 10 CFR 20.1301(a)(1), exclusive of the listed contributions (background, medical administration, § 35.75 released patients, voluntary medical research, sanitary sewerage disposal).
- In any one hour in an unrestricted area: 0.002 rem (0.02 mSv) from external sources, 10 CFR 20.1301(a)(2), excluding dose contributions from § 35.75-released patients.

10. CURRENCY NOTE
These figures are current as of the eCFR edition fetched 2026-11-17. Part 20 has an open revision effort at the NRC; the values above are the codified ones and any change would appear as an amendment to 20.1301. Verify 20.1301 against the then-current eCFR before relying on these numbers in a licensing submittal, and check whether the licensee holds any 20.1301(d) authorization, which would raise that site's applicable annual figure to as much as 0.5 rem (5 mSv).

question: H2
answer:
COMPLIANCE MEMO — ALCOHOL CONCENTRATION BAR FOR SAFETY-SENSITIVE DUTY (US CMV DRIVERS)

1. ANSWER
A US commercial motor vehicle driver is barred from performing safety-sensitive functions at an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater. 0.04 is the federal threshold; the prohibition attaches at exactly 0.04, not above it.

Authority: 49 CFR 382.201 — "No driver shall report for duty or remain on duty requiring the performance of safety-sensitive functions while having an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater. No employer having knowledge that a driver has an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater shall permit the driver to perform or continue to perform safety-sensitive functions." (66 FR 43103, as amended at 77 FR 4483.)

2. UNIT AND MEASUREMENT
- Part 40's standard method is evidential breath testing (EBT); results are reported as alcohol concentration in grams of alcohol per 210 liters of breath (g/210 L). 0.04 g/210 L is numerically equivalent to 0.04% BAC, so the figure is the same either way it is spoken.
- An EBT must be able to distinguish alcohol from acetone at the 0.02 level (FMCSA Implementation Guidelines, Ch. 7), which is why the 0.02 line matters operationally as well as substantively.
- Where blood testing is authorized (limited circumstances, principally post-accident), results are expressed as grams per 100 mL (g/dL), i.e., percent by weight; 0.04% is the same threshold.
- A confirmation test is required before a result is treated as a violation (Part 40 Subpart C); the 0.04 figure applies to the confirmed result.

3. THE TWO-BAND STRUCTURE — DO NOT CONFLATE
The federal rules set two distinct numbers. Only one of them is a bar from safety-sensitive duty in the full sense.

| Confirmed alcohol concentration | Regulatory effect | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| 0.04 or greater | Prohibited concentration. Driver shall not report for or remain on duty in safety-sensitive functions; employer shall not permit it. Treated as a violation: immediate removal from safety-sensitive functions, referral to a Substance Abuse Professional, SAP evaluation and compliance with the SAP's recommendations, and no return to safety-sensitive duty until a return-to-duty test shows less than 0.02. Also reportable to the FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse as an alcohol violation. | 49 CFR 382.201; 382.503; 382.309; 382.501 |
| 0.02 or greater but less than 0.04 | Not a prohibited concentration, but the driver shall not perform or continue to perform safety-sensitive functions (including driving a CMV), and the employer shall not permit it, until the start of the driver's next regularly scheduled duty period, and in no event less than 24 hours after administration of the test. No SAP referral required; this is a temporary removal, not a Part 382 violation. | 49 CFR 382.505(a) |
| Less than 0.02 | May return to / perform safety-sensitive functions (subject to the return-to-duty requirement above if the driver is in the SAP process). | 49 CFR 382.309 |

Guardrail against a common error: 0.02 is not the answer to "at what concentration is the driver barred." 0.02-0.04 is a mandatory 24-hour-plus stand-down; 0.04 is the prohibited concentration with the full consequence chain. Conversely, do not describe the 0.04 consequence as a "24-hour removal" — removal at 0.04 or greater is open-ended until SAP evaluation and a return-to-duty result below 0.02.

4. WHAT COUNTS AS REACHING THE THRESHOLD
- Reporting for duty, or remaining on duty, in a safety-sensitive function with a confirmed 0.04 or greater — including driving a CMV. 382.201.
- Refusal to submit to a required alcohol test (pre-employment controlled-substance, post-accident, random, reasonable suspicion, return-to-duty, follow-up) is treated as a refusal and carries the same consequences as a 0.04 or greater result — removal from safety-sensitive functions, SAP process, and Clearinghouse reporting. 382.211; 382.503.
- Independent prohibitions that do not depend on any measured concentration: use of alcohol while performing safety-sensitive functions (382.205); performing safety-sensitive functions within four hours after using alcohol (382.207); use of alcohol within eight hours following an accident requiring a post-accident test, or until the post-accident test is taken, whichever comes first (382.209). A driver can be in violation at a concentration below 0.04 on these grounds.

5. SCOPE AND CAVEATS
- This is the federal minimum applicable to drivers operating CMVs requiring a CDL who are subject to Part 382. It is a floor, not a ceiling: 382.505(b) expressly preserves an employer's authority independent of Part 382 to act on results below 0.04, and state law or company policy may impose a stricter threshold (including zero tolerance). Where a client's policy is stricter, the stricter number governs that client's drivers.
- The threshold applies across testing modes (random, reasonable suspicion, post-accident, return-to-duty, follow-up) because 382.201 is stated in terms of reporting for or remaining on duty; the mode affects the testing procedure and timing, not the 0.04 line. Post-accident testing has its own time windows (test within 2 hours where practicable, cease attempts after 8 hours) but the same 0.04 prohibited concentration.
- An employer with actual knowledge of a 0.04 or greater result, or of on-duty/pre-duty use, must not permit the driver to perform safety-sensitive functions; permitting it is itself a violation subject to civil penalties under 49 U.S.C. 521(b). 382.201; 382.507.
- Violations of Part 40 testing procedures are separately subject to the same penalty provisions. 382.507.

6. ONE-LINE CITABLE STATEMENT FOR A POLICY OR TRAINING DOCUMENT
"No driver shall report for duty or remain on duty requiring the performance of safety-sensitive functions while having an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater (49 CFR 382.201). A driver with a confirmed alcohol concentration of 0.02 or greater but less than 0.04 shall not perform safety-sensitive functions until the start of the next regularly scheduled duty period, but not less than 24 hours after the test (49 CFR 382.505(a))."

question: H4
answer:
Statutory answer for Great Britain (England, Scotland and Wales), current law:

1. Paid annual leave entitlement: 5.6 weeks per leave year.
2. Statutory cap: 28 days per leave year.

Legal basis
- Working Time Regulations 1998 (SI 1998/1833), regulation 13: a worker is entitled to 5.6 weeks' paid annual leave in each leave year (for leave years beginning on or after 1 April 2009).
- Regulation 13A: a worker's leave entitlement under regulation 13 shall not exceed 28 days in any leave year.

How the cap operates

| Working pattern | 5.6-week calculation | Statutory entitlement |
|---|---:|---:|
| 5 days per week | 5.6 × 5 = 28 | 28 days |
| 6 days per week | 5.6 × 6 = 33.6 | 28 days (capped) |
| 3 days per week | 5.6 × 3 = 16.8 | 16.8 days |
| Compressed hours | Lower of 28 days or 5.6 × days worked per week | 28 days maximum, with each day being the average working day |

The 28-day figure is a ceiling on the statutory 5.6-week entitlement, not an additional allowance. It bites where a worker's working week exceeds five days: for example, a six-day-per-week worker would otherwise accrue 33.6 days but is limited to 28 days.

Key practical points for HR
- 'Worker' is used in the broad statutory sense. The entitlement covers employees, agency workers, casual and zero-hours workers, irregular-hours workers and part-year workers, subject to the statutory accrual rules.
- Part-time workers receive 5.6 weeks pro rata, so their entitlement is the lower of 28 days or 5.6 × their normal days worked per week. The 28-day cap is not a minimum for part-time workers.
- Bank and public holidays are not a separate statutory paid entitlement in addition to the 5.6 weeks. An employer may include bank holidays within the statutory 5.6 weeks; if it does, those days count towards the 28-day total.
- Contractual leave above the statutory minimum is not limited by the 28-day cap. An employer can provide more than 28 days under the contract, but the statutory floor remains 5.6 weeks and the statutory ceiling on that floor is 28 days.
- The 28-day cap is expressed in days of the worker's normal working pattern, not in calendar days and not as a fixed number of hours. For workers with compressed or variable days, the cap is applied as 28 days of the average working day.

Bottom line: the statutory minimum is 5.6 weeks, and the statutory maximum/cap is 28 days.

question: H6
answer:
SIZE LIMITS IN THE ORIGINAL DNS SPECIFICATION (RFC 1034 / RFC 1035, 1987)

ANSWER
  - A single label: at most 63 octets (0-63; the zero-length label is reserved for the root).
  - A full domain name: at most 255 octets in wire format, where that 255 counts every label's data octets PLUS every label's one-octet length field PLUS the final zero octet of the root.

1. NORMATIVE TEXT

1.1 RFC 1035, Section 2.3.4 ("Size limits")
    "labels          63 octets or less
     names           255 octets or less
     TTL             positive values of a signed 32 bit number.
     UDP messages    512 octets or less"

1.2 RFC 1035, Section 3.1 ("Name space definitions") - this is the operative
    wire-format statement and defines what the 255 counts:
    "Each label is represented as a one octet length field followed by that
     number of octets.  Since every domain name ends with the null label of
     the root, a domain name is terminated by a length byte of zero.  The
     high order two bits of every length octet must be zero, and the
     remaining six bits of the length field limit the label to 63 octets or
     less.
     To simplify implementations, the total length of a domain name (i.e.,
     label octets and label length octets) is restricted to 255 octets or
     less."

    Two facts fall out of this paragraph:
      (a) The 63-octet label cap is not arbitrary - it is forced by the
          encoding. The length octet spends its top two bits on the
          compression-pointer escape (11) and reserved values (10, 01), so
          only six bits remain: 2^6 - 1 = 63.
      (b) The 255-octet name cap is explicitly defined as "label octets and
          label length octets", i.e. the wire form, and the terminating zero
          octet is part of that count.

1.3 RFC 1034, Section 3.1 ("Name space definitions")
    "Each node has a label, which is zero to 63 octets in length."
    "To simplify implementations, the total number of octets that represent a
     domain name (i.e., the sum of all label octets and label lengths) is
     limited to 255."

1.4 RFC 1035, Section 3.5 ("Preferred name syntax") - a separate, weaker
    statement about textual host names, not the wire limit:
    "Labels must be 63 characters or less."
    This is the "preferred syntax" for host names, later relaxed; RFC 2181 and
    RFC 9499 confirm that the preferred syntax is not mandatory and that the
    real, protocol-level limits are the octet limits above.

2. RESTATEMENTS (confirming the original figures were never revised)

  RFC 2181, Section 11: "The length of any one label is limited to between 1
  and 63 octets.  A full domain name is limited to 255 octets (including the
  separators)."

  RFC 9499, Section 2: "The length of each label is between 0 and 63 octets
  inclusive... A domain name in the global DNS has a maximum total length of
  255 octets in the wire format; the root represents one octet for this
  calculation."

  (RFC 9499 also notes that Multicast DNS, RFC 6762, reads RFC 1035 as 255
  octets of name content plus a separate terminating zero byte. That is a
  divergent reading used by mDNS only; the global-DNS reading, and the one in
  the original text, is that the root's zero octet is inside the 255.)

3. WHAT THE 255 ACTUALLY BUYS YOU - WORKED ARITHMETIC

  For a name of n labels with data lengths L1..Ln, the wire length is:

      wire = SUM(Li) + n + 1        (n length octets, plus the root's zero)

  subject to  wire <= 255  and  Li <= 63 for every i.

  Maximum total label data therefore depends on how many labels you use:

    n = 1 : data <= min(63, 255-2)   = 63   -> wire =  1 + 63 + 1 =  65
    n = 3 : data <= min(189, 255-4)  = 189  -> wire =  3 + 189 + 1 = 193
    n = 4 : data <= min(252, 255-5)  = 250  -> wire =  4 + 250 + 1 = 255  (tight)
    n = 127: data <= min(8001, 255-128) = 127 -> wire = 127 + 127 + 1 = 255 (tight)

  Note the n = 4 case carefully, because it is where a naive reading goes
  wrong: four full 63-octet labels give 252 + 4 + 1 = 257 octets, which
  EXCEEDS the 255-octet limit. The longest legal four-label name is
  63.63.63.61 (data 250 octets). The absolute maximum amount of label data in
  any legal name is 250 octets.

  Presentation format is a different count and must not be confused with
  octets. The name above is written with three dots:
      63 + 1 + 63 + 1 + 63 + 1 + 61 = 253 characters (254 with a trailing
      root dot).
  So the frequently quoted "253 characters" is the presentation-form figure
  for the same name that occupies 255 octets on the wire; it is not a second,
  competing limit. The apparent 2-octet gap is exactly the four length octets
  minus the three dots plus the root's zero octet (255 - 4 + 3 - 1 + ... in
  short: 250 data + 3 dots = 253 characters; 250 data + 4 length octets + 1
  root = 255 octets).

4. SCOPE NOTES

  - Compression: the RFC 1035 Section 4.1.4 pointer scheme lets a name in a
    message be replaced by a 2-octet pointer or by labels ending in a pointer.
    Compression changes how many octets a name OCCUPIES in a message; it does
    not change the 63/255 limits on the name itself.
  - Octets vs characters: the limits are on octets. Labels may hold arbitrary
    8-bit values (RFC 1035 Section 3.1, reaffirmed by RFC 2181 Section 11), so
    for non-ASCII or escaped content the character count in presentation form
    can exceed the octet count.
  - Octets vs message size: the 255-octet name limit and the 512-octet UDP
    message limit (RFC 1035 Section 2.3.4, raised by EDNS0) are independent
    constraints.
  - Nothing in RFC 1123, RFC 2181, or the EDNS-era documents changed either
    figure; the only substantive later changes were to the permitted
    CHARACTER SET (RFC 1123 allowing a leading digit, RFC 2181/RFC 6055
    allowing arbitrary binary labels), not to the lengths.

5. ONE-LINE CITABLE FORM

  RFC 1035 Section 2.3.4: labels 63 octets or less; names 255 octets or less -
  the 255 being the wire-format total of label data, label length octets, and
  the root's terminating zero octet (RFC 1035 Section 3.1).

question: H8
answer:
US FEDERAL MAXIMUM CONTAMINANT LEVEL (MCL) FOR PFOA IN DRINKING WATER

=== 1. ANSWER ===

The federal MCL for perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) is 4.0 parts per trillion (ppt), which is identically 4.0 nanograms per litre (ng/L).

As the rule itself lists it, in 40 CFR § 141.61(c)(2), table 'MCLs and HBWCs for PFAS', the entry is:

  (vi) 45285-51-6   PFOA   0.0000040        Not applicable.

where the column heading is 'MCL (mg/l) (unless otherwise noted)' and the second column shown is 'HBWC (mg/l) for Hazard Index calculation'. So the rule-listed value is 0.0000040 mg/L; EPA's own summary of the same rule expresses it as '4.0 parts per trillion (ppt) (also expressed as ng/L)'.

=== 2. UNIT CONVERSION, SHOWN EXPLICITLY ===

From the rule's mg/L figure:
  0.0000040 mg/L x (1,000,000 ng / 1 mg) = 4.0 ng/L
  (equivalently 0.0000040 mg/L = 4.0e-6 mg/L = 4.0e-9 g/L = 4.0 ng/L)

From the rule's ppt figure (drinking water, density ~1.00 kg/L):
  4.0 parts per trillion = 4.0 x 1e-12 mass fraction
  1 L of water ~ 1.0 kg = 1.0e9 ng, so 4.0 x 1e-12 x 1.0e9 ng/L = 4.0 ng/L
  1 ppt = 1 ng/L for water; therefore 4.0 ppt = 4.0 ng/L.

Complete set of equivalent expressions of the same MCL (all consistent, use whichever the reader needs):
  0.0000040 mg/L
  0.0040 µg/L
  4.0 ng/L
  4.0 ppt
  4,000 pg/L

The rule value carries two significant figures (4.0), and the conversion to ng/L preserves that precision; do not restate it as '4 ng/L' or '4.00 ng/L' — 4.0 is the correct rounding and matches the practical quantitation level (see §4 below).

=== 3. SOURCE CITATION AND REGULATORY IDENTITY ===

- Regulation: National Primary Drinking Water Regulations, 40 CFR Part 141, Subpart G, § 141.61(c) — 'Maximum contaminant levels for organic contaminants', paragraph (c)(2) 'MCLs and HBWCs for PFAS', item (vi), PFOA, CAS 45285-51-6.
- Promulgating rule: PFAS National Primary Drinking Water Regulation, final rule published at 89 FR 32532 (Federal Register document 2024-07773, 26 April 2024), with a correction at 89 FR 49102 (11 June 2024); eCFR amendment notes to § 141.61 read '89 FR 32744, Apr. 26, 2024; 89 FR 49102, June 11, 2024'.
- Statutory basis: Safe Drinking Water Act § 1412; the rule also sets a non-enforceable Maximum Contaminant Level Goal (MCLG) for PFOA of zero.
- Effective/compliance date for the PFAS MCLs: § 141.61(a)(4) states 'The effective date for § 141.61(c)(2)(i) through (vii) is April 26, 2029' — i.e., the PFOA MCL is promulgated and in the Code of Federal Regulations, with the compliance date for the listed PFAS paragraphs set at 26 April 2029.

=== 4. INTERNAL CONSISTENCY CHECKS AGAINST OTHER NUMBERS IN THE SAME RULE ===

These are the numbers in the deliverable's own source that could contradict a mis-stated MCL; each is reconciled:

- Monitoring trigger level, PFOA = 2.0 ng/L (§ 141.142(b)(5) table, Subpart Z). The MCL (4.0 ng/L) is twice the trigger level, which is the correct relationship: the trigger is the lower, non-enforcement action level that forces quarterly monitoring, not the MCL. 4.0 > 2.0 — consistent. Do not report 2.0 ng/L as the MCL.
- Practical Quantitation Level (PQL), PFOA = 4.0 ppt (§ 141.142(f)(1)(iv), Table 1 to that paragraph). The PQL equals the MCL, so a laboratory can quantify at the MCL itself; the PQL is not a separate or higher standard. 4.0 = 4.0 — consistent. (Same for PFOS at 4.0 ppt; HFPO-DA 5.0, PFNA 4.0, PFBS and PFHxS 3.0 ppt — none of these is the PFOA MCL.)
- HBWC for PFOA = 'Not applicable'. PFOA is NOT a component of the PFAS Mixture Hazard Index (the HI covers HFPO-DA, PFBS, PFHxS, PFNA only). Therefore no health-based water concentration (10 ng/L for PFHxS, PFNA, HFPO-DA; 2,000 ng/L for PFBS) applies to PFOA, and the unitless Hazard Index of 1 must not be presented as a PFOA limit. Consistent — the deliverable states no HBWC for PFOA.
- MCLG for PFOA = zero. Zero is a non-enforceable health goal, not the MCL; it is not the answer to this question and is not used in any calculation here. Consistent.
- Companion MCLs, for disambiguation only: PFOS 4.0 ppt (same as PFOA); PFHxS 10 ppt, PFNA 10 ppt, HFPO-DA (GenX) 10 ppt; PFBS has no individual MCL; PFAS mixtures of two or more of PFHxS, PFNA, HFPO-DA and PFBS are limited by a unitless Hazard Index MCL of 1. None of these is the PFOA MCL; they are listed here only so the 4.0 figure is not confused with the 10 ppt values or the unitless HI.

=== 5. STATUS AND WHAT WOULD CHANGE THIS ANSWER ===

This answer reflects the eCFR text of 40 CFR § 141.61 as fetched on 2026-11-17, which lists PFOA at 0.0000040 mg/L and still carries the 26 April 2029 effective/compliance date for paragraphs (c)(2)(i)–(vii). No amendment reflected in that snapshot alters the PFOA value. PFAS drinking-water regulation has been actively litigated and reconsidered, so before relying on this figure for a compliance decision, re-verify the current text of § 141.61(c)(2)(vi) at ecfr.gov and the docket at EPA's PFAS NPDWR page; the answer changes only if a future amendment revises the PFOA row or a court vacates it. If a different value appears in a later snapshot, the rule text — not this document — governs.

=== 6. SCOPE NOTES ===

- This is the US federal MCL under the Safe Drinking Water Act. State standards are different and are not the federal MCL: for example, Pennsylvania's state rule sets PFOA at 14 ng/L (MCLG 8 ng/L). Do not substitute a state number.
- Distinguish the MCL (4.0 ng/L, enforceable) from: the MCLG (zero, non-enforceable health goal), EPA drinking-water health advisories (non-enforceable, non-regulatory advisory values), and the 2.0 ng/L monitoring trigger level (an action level for increased monitoring, not a limit).
- Applies to community water systems and non-transient, non-community water systems, consistent with Part 141 Subpart G.
