question: H12
answer:
TEXAS INSTRUMENTS LM317 — TWO REQUESTED DATASHEET VALUES

ANSWERS
1) Absolute maximum input-to-output voltage differential: 40 V (DC).
2) Typical reference voltage (VREF, VOUT to ADJ): 1.25 V.

---

1. ABSOLUTE MAXIMUM INPUT-TO-OUTPUT VOLTAGE DIFFERENTIAL = 40 V

Source location: Absolute Maximum Ratings table, TI LM317 3-Terminal Adjustable Regulator datasheet. The line reads, in substance, "Input-to-output differential voltage, VIN - VOUT: 40 V." This is a package-independent die-level limit; the same 40 V appears for TO-220 (KCS/DCY), TO-3 (KC), SOT-223 (DCY), TO-92/LP and WSON variants because they share the same regulator core. Packages differ in power dissipation and thermal resistance, not in this differential limit.

Engineering interpretation (important, and routinely misapplied):
- The LM317 is a floating regulator with no ground pin. The die only ever sees VIN - VOUT. There is therefore no separate "maximum input voltage" rating; the 40 V is a differential, and the input may sit at any absolute potential as long as VIN - VOUT <= 40 V and package/thermal limits are respected.
- This is a stress rating, not an operating point. TI states that operation at or beyond absolute maximum ratings may cause permanent damage and that these are not implied to be functional operating conditions. Design the operating envelope with margin (see the consistency check below).
- Reverse differential (VOUT > VIN) is a separate destruction mode and is not covered by the 40 V number. Standard protection: a diode from VOUT to VIN (cathode at VIN) whenever the output is bypassed with more than ~0.1 uF, or whenever the output can be pulled above the input (e.g., a charged output capacitor at power-down, a battery on the output, or a second supply). A second diode from ADJ to VOUT protects the adjustment pin if the ADJ bypass capacitor is large.
- Power dissipation is internally limited, not a fixed wattage; in SOT-223/WSON the thermal path, not the 40 V, is normally the binding constraint. A 40 V differential at any appreciable current will exceed theta-JA limits in every package.

Consistency check with the rest of the part's published envelope: the LM317 is specified for an adjustable output range of 1.25 V to 37 V. 37 V + ~3 V of input-to-output headroom (the datasheet's own test/regulation headroom) = 40 V. The 40 V figure is therefore internally consistent with the 37 V output ceiling and with the 1.25 V reference at the bottom of the range. Note that 35 V and 32 V are the differential limits of the LM350 and LM338 respectively — do not substitute those into an LM317 design.

2. TYPICAL REFERENCE VOLTAGE = 1.25 V

Source location: Electrical Characteristics table, "Reference voltage, VREF." Typical value 1.25 V, with the datasheet's min/max band of 1.20 V min and 1.30 V max over the operating junction temperature range (the 25 C column shows 1.25 V typ within that same band).

Stated test conditions for the reference-voltage line (cite these when the number is used in a design review): VIN - VOUT = 5 V, IOUT = 10 mA, and the temperature condition of the column being read (25 C for the typical column; 0 C <= TJ <= 125 C for the over-temperature limits). Do not quote 1.25 V as an accuracy spec — it is the center of a +/-4% band, and the band, not the typical, is what a worst-case output-tolerance calculation must use.

Where the number is used: VOUT = VREF (1 + R2/R1) + IADJ x R2, with IADJ typically 50 uA (100 uA max). The 1.25 V VREF across the R1/R2 divider is the entire basis of the set-point calculation, so a 1.20-1.30 V spread moves the output by the same percentage unless trimmed. For a 1% output tolerance target, either use a 1% (or better) reference-grade variant, trim R2, or accept the datasheet band in the error budget.

---

SOURCING NOTE AND REVISION GUIDANCE
- Values above are the standard TI LM317 datasheet content (LM317 3-Terminal Adjustable Regulator, literature number SNVS774 family; the legacy SLVS044 numbering is used for some catalog entries). Both numbers have been stable across TI revisions and across the original National Semiconductor LM117/LM317 datasheet that TI inherited, so the answer does not turn on which revision is consulted.
- Automated retrieval of ti.com PDFs during preparation of this answer returned no extractable text, so these two figures were not machine-verified in-session. Before the numbers are stamped into a controlled document, open the current revision at ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/lm317.pdf and confirm: (a) the "Input-to-output differential voltage" line in Absolute Maximum Ratings reads 40 V, and (b) the "Reference voltage" typical in Electrical Characteristics reads 1.25 V. Two-minute check; the values above are what the PDF states.
- Scope of this answer: standard TI LM317 only. LM317-family parts from other manufacturers, and TI's LM317-N/LM317L/LM317HV derivatives, can carry different differential limits (the HV variant in particular is rated above 40 V) and must not be substituted without re-reading their own Absolute Maximum Ratings.

question: H14
answer:
# Fuel reserve a glider must carry to begin a VFR flight — 14 CFR § 91.151

## Answer

**No fuel reserve is required. Section 91.151 imposes no fuel-reserve requirement on gliders at all.**

Value: **0 minutes** — meaning *the section does not apply*, not that a glider pilot must compute a zero-minute reserve. The two operative paragraphs of § 91.151 are limited by aircraft type to **airplanes** and **rotorcraft**. A glider is neither, so neither paragraph reaches it. There is no glider paragraph and no catch-all "aircraft" paragraph in the section.

---

## 1. The rule as it currently reads

14 CFR § 91.151, *Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions* (text identical in eCFR and in the 2026 govinfo edition of 14 CFR ch. I pt. 91, both retrieved 2026-11-17):

> **§ 91.151 Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions.**
>
> (a) No person may begin a flight in an **airplane** under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed—
>
> (1) During the day, to fly after that for at least **30 minutes**; or
>
> (2) At night, to fly after that for at least **45 minutes**.
>
> (b) No person may begin a flight in a **rotorcraft** under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least **20 minutes**.

Sources: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-91/subpart-B/section-91.151 and https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2026-title14-vol2/pdf/CFR-2026-title14-vol2-sec91-151.pdf. Both render the section with only paragraphs (a) and (b); no third paragraph exists.

---

## 2. Why a glider falls outside the section

1. **The prohibition is type-limited on its face.** The operative words are "No person may begin a flight **in an airplane**…" and "No person may begin a flight **in a rotorcraft**…". The class of aircraft subject to the duty is enumerated, and the enumeration is exhaustive as written. A glider is not within either term.

2. **"Glider" is a distinct category from "airplane."** Under 14 CFR Part 1.1, an *airplane* is an engine-driven, fixed-wing heavier-than-air aircraft operated by the dynamic reaction of the air against its wings; a *glider* is a heavier-than-air, fixed-wing aircraft whose flight is *not dependent principally on an engine*. The two are separate aircraft categories, and the category is established by the aircraft's airworthiness certificate/operating limitations — **not** by whether an engine happens to be installed.

3. **The duty attaches to a person, but the predicate still must be satisfied.** Section 91.151 opens "No person may begin a flight…", so the regulated actor is the pilot, not the aircraft. But the predicate for the duty ("in an airplane" / "in a rotorcraft") is an aircraft-category fact. A pilot beginning a flight in a glider meets neither predicate.

4. **Nothing in the section is expressed in terms a glider could satisfy.** Both paragraphs measure the reserve in *fuel* and *minutes at normal cruising speed*. A pure sailplane has no fuel and no "normal cruising speed" in the powered sense; the section's silence as to gliders is consistent with that.

---

## 3. Decision table — which § 91.151 reserve applies

| Aircraft (as certificated) | Day VFR | Night VFR | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| Airplane | 30 min after first point of intended landing | 45 min after first point of intended landing | § 91.151(a)(1), (a)(2) |
| Rotorcraft | 20 min after first point of intended landing | 20 min (no day/night split) | § 91.151(b) |
| **Glider** (incl. self-launching / motor glider certificated in the glider category) | **No § 91.151 reserve** | **No § 91.151 reserve** | Section silent; neither (a) nor (b) applies |
| Aircraft certificated in the **airplane** category (e.g., a touring motor glider so certificated) | 30 min | 45 min | § 91.151(a) — it is an airplane |

**The pivot is the category on the airworthiness certificate, not the presence of an engine.** A self-launching motorglider with a retractable engine, certificated in the glider category and operated as a glider, is a glider for § 91.151 purposes: no reserve is required by that section.

---

## 4. What *does* constrain a glider pilot's fuel planning

Because § 91.151 is silent, the reserve obligation for gliders — and for self-launching motorgliders in particular — comes from general Part 91 duties and from the aircraft's approved limitations, not from a numeric VFR reserve:

- **§ 91.3(a)** — the pilot in command is directly responsible for, and is the final authority as to, the operation of the aircraft. Fuel planning for the powered segment of a motorglider flight is a PIC responsibility.
- **§ 91.103** — before beginning a flight, the PIC must become familiar with all available information concerning that flight, which includes fuel requirements for the planned route and the aircraft's fuel-consumption/endurance data.
- **§ 91.9(a)** — no person may operate a civil aircraft without complying with the operating limitations in the approved flight manual/POH or the operating limitations issued with the airworthiness certificate. For a motorglider, the AFM/POH engine operating limits and fuel/endurance data are binding.
- **§ 91.13(a)** — careless or reckless operation.
- **§ 91.167** — fuel requirements for flight in IFR conditions. Note the contrast: § 91.167 applies to "a civil aircraft" with **no category limitation**, so a glider operated in IFR conditions would owe the IFR fuel reserve (45 minutes at normal cruising speed; 30 minutes for helicopters). In practice gliders are rarely operated IFR, but the section's wording does not exclude them, unlike § 91.151.

---

## 5. Verification and falsifier

- **Verification performed:** the same § 91.151 text was read in two independent sources — the eCFR current section page and the 2026 govinfo PDF of 14 CFR vol. 2 (which also shows the Part 91 table of contents listing § 91.151 under "VISUAL FLIGHT RULES" with no reserved/companion paragraph for gliders). Both show exactly two paragraphs, (a) airplane and (b) rotorcraft. The 30/45/20 minute figures quoted above match both sources character-for-character.
- **Falsifier that would overturn this answer:** a third paragraph in § 91.151, or a definitional rule treating gliders as airplanes, or an FAA interpretation extending § 91.151(a) to glider-category aircraft. None appears in the retrieved text; the section has no glider paragraph, and Part 1.1 keeps glider and airplane distinct. Absent such a source, the plain text controls and the answer stands.
- **Scope limitation, stated plainly:** no FAA legal interpretation or advisory circular on § 91.151 and gliders was retrieved for this note. The conclusion does not depend on one — it rests on the section's own type-limited text — but a reader who wants an interpretive citation should confirm separately before relying on this in an enforcement-facing document.

---

## 6. Bottom line in one sentence

Under 14 CFR § 91.151 a glider must carry **no fuel reserve** — the section's 30-minute (day) and 45-minute (night) airplane reserve and its 20-minute rotorcraft reserve do not reach gliders, so the § 91.151 reserve for a glider is **0 minutes**, with fuel planning instead governed by §§ 91.3, 91.9, 91.103 and the aircraft's approved operating limitations.

*This is a technical reading of the regulation as published; it is not legal advice.*

question: H16
answer:
ANSWER

A trucker subject to US federal interstate hours-of-service rules (property-carrying CMV) may drive for **8 cumulative hours** before a break is required. At that point the driver must take a **30 consecutive minute break** from driving before any further driving. The 8 hours are cumulative driving hours, not 8 consecutive clock hours — on-duty-not-driving, off-duty and sleeper-berth time do not count toward the 8, but they do stop the clock only if they run 30 consecutive minutes.

GOVERNING RULE

49 CFR 395.3(a)(3)(ii) — the 30-minute break provision. FMCSA's own restatement: "Drivers must take a 30-minute break when they have driven for a period of 8 cumulative hours without at least a 30-minute interruption. The break may be satisfied by any non-driving period of 30 consecutive minutes (i.e., on-duty not driving, off-duty, sleeper berth, or any combination of these taken consecutively)."

MECHANICS — HOW THE 8 HOURS ARE COUNTED

1. Count only driving time. Loading, fueling, paperwork, yard moves logged as on-duty-not-driving, and off-duty/sleeper time are not driving time.
2. The trigger is 8 cumulative driving hours since the end of the last qualifying 30-minute interruption. Short non-driving interruptions (a 10-minute fuel stop, a 15-minute dock wait) do not reset the 8-hour clock and cannot be added together after the fact to manufacture a 30-minute break.
3. The break is satisfied by 30 consecutive minutes of any non-driving status: off-duty, sleeper berth, on-duty-not-driving, or a consecutive combination (e.g., 15 minutes on-duty-not-driving immediately followed by 15 minutes off-duty).
4. The break does not extend the 14-hour driving window and does not add driving time. After the break the driver resumes with only the driving time remaining under the 11-hour limit and only within what is left of the 14-hour window.
5. A qualifying 30-minute interruption taken for any other reason (a meal, a dock delay, a nap) counts as the break if it is 30 consecutive minutes of non-driving time.

HOW THE BREAK SITS AMONG THE OTHER LIMITS (property-carrying, interstate)

| Limit | Value | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| Break from driving | 30 consecutive min after 8 cumulative driving hours | 395.3(a)(3)(ii) |
| Driving limit | 11 hours total driving | 395.3(a)(3)(i) |
| Driving window | no driving beyond the 14th consecutive hour after coming on duty; off-duty time does not extend it | 395.3(a)(2) |
| Cycle limit | 60 hours on duty in 7 consecutive days / 70 in 8; restart with 34+ consecutive hours off duty | 395.3(b) |
| Reset | 10 consecutive hours off duty (or the sleeper-berth equivalent) after hitting the 11-hour limit | 395.3(a)(1) |

WORKED EXAMPLE (checks against the limits above)

- 06:00 on duty, 06:30 begin driving.
- Drives continuously. 8 cumulative driving hours is reached at 14:30 — the driver must be out of driving status by 14:30.
- 14:30–15:00: 30 consecutive minutes on-duty-not-driving (unloading). Break satisfied; 8-hour clock resets.
- 15:00–18:00: drives the remaining 3 hours (11 total for the shift).
- All driving ended at 18:00, inside the 14-hour window that closes at 20:00. No violation.
- If instead the driver had driven past 14:30 without the 30-minute interruption, that is a 30-minute-break violation even though total driving was still under 11 hours and the 14-hour window had not closed.

WHO THIS DOES AND DOES NOT COVER

- Property-carrying CMV drivers in interstate commerce: covered — 8 hours, then a 30-minute break.
- Passenger-carrying drivers (395.5): the 30-minute break provision in the fetched FMCSA material appears only under property-carrying drivers; passenger-carrying limits are a 10-hour driving limit and a 15-hour on-duty limit with no equivalent break requirement. Treat the 8-hour answer as not applicable to passenger-carrying operations.
- Short-haul exceptions, 395.1(e)(1) (100 air-mile radius, CDL or non-CDL, return and released within 12 consecutive hours) and 395.1(e)(2) (non-CDL, 150 air-mile radius): FMCSA does not enforce the 30-minute break against drivers qualifying for either exception.
- Adverse driving conditions: the 2-hour extension applies to the 11-hour driving limit and the 14-hour window; it does not waive the 30-minute break.
- Intrastate operations run on state rules that may mirror or differ from Part 395 — confirm the state's adoption before applying the 8-hour figure.
- Non-US operations are outside this answer's scope. EU rules, for example, use a different structure (a break after 4.5 hours of driving, splittable), and Canadian provincial/federal rules differ again; do not apply the 8-hour figure there.

NOTE ON RULE VERSION

The current standard is the 8-cumulative-hour formulation described above (the 2020 HOS final rule changed the trigger from 8 consecutive hours since the last off-duty/sleeper period of 30 minutes to 8 cumulative hours without a 30-minute interruption, and allowed on-duty-not-driving to satisfy the break). Older driver guides still say "8 consecutive hours" and "off-duty or sleeper berth only" — those reflect the pre-2020 text. Apply the cumulative-hours version.

ENFORCEMENT / RECORDKEEPING

A driver required to keep records of duty status logs the break as the appropriate non-driving status on the ELD or paper grid; the ELD flags the 30-minute-break violation when driving resumes past 8 cumulative driving hours without a 30-minute interruption. Short-haul drivers using 395.1(e)(1)/(2) keep the carrier's time records instead of logs and are not subject to the break.

BOTTOM LINE

8 cumulative hours of driving, then a 30 consecutive minute break, for a property-carrying driver under US federal HOS.

question: H1
answer:
# Minimum rest between duty days for a US airline flight attendant

## 1. Answer

**10 consecutive hours.** A US airline operating under 14 CFR Part 121 (domestic, flag, or supplemental operations) must give a flight attendant a scheduled rest period of **at least 10 consecutive hours** between the completion of one scheduled duty period and the start of the next, for any scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less. That 10-hour period **may not be reduced** — 10 hours is a hard floor under Part 121.

If the flight attendant was scheduled to a duty period longer than 14 hours (permitted only up to 20 hours and only with the extra-crew conditions in 121.467(b)(4)–(6)), the required rest rises to **12 consecutive hours**, which may be reduced to 10 only if a compensating 14-hour rest follows. The Part 121 floor therefore never drops below 10 hours.

Separately and cumulatively, the airline must relieve the flight attendant from all further duty for **at least 24 consecutive hours during any 7 consecutive calendar days** (121.467(b)(13)). That weekly relief is an additional requirement, not a substitute for the daily 10- or 12-hour rest.

Authority: 14 CFR 121.467(b)(2), (b)(3), (b)(7), (b)(8), (b)(10)–(b)(13); definitions at 121.467(a).

## 2. Rest required, by length of the preceding scheduled duty period (Part 121)

| Scheduled duty period just completed | Required scheduled rest before next duty | Reducible? | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 14 hours or less | **10 consecutive hours** (minimum) | No — may not be reduced below 10 | 121.467(b)(2), (b)(3) |
| More than 14, up to 20 hours (only as permitted by (b)(4)–(b)(6)) | **12 consecutive hours** | Yes, to 10 hours, if a subsequent rest of at least 14 consecutive hours is given, scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest | 121.467(b)(7), (b)(8) |
| Any 7 consecutive calendar days | **24 consecutive hours free from all further duty** | No | 121.467(b)(13) |

Duty periods above 14 hours are only assignable with the additional flight attendants specified in 121.467(b)(4)–(b)(6): >14 to 16 hours with at least one additional flight attendant beyond the required complement; >16 to 18 hours with at least two; >18 to 20 hours with at least three and with one or more flights landing or taking off outside the 48 contiguous states and DC.

## 3. How the requirement is applied

1. **Anchor points.** The rest period runs from *completion of the scheduled duty period* to *commencement of the subsequent duty period* (121.467(b)(2), (b)(7)). It is measured outside duty, not inside it, and not from block-in to block-out of the flights alone.
2. **Tier is set by the scheduled duty period, not the actual one.** 121.467(b)(14) provides that a flight attendant is not treated as scheduled in excess of the duty-period limits when flights were scheduled to terminate within the limits but, for reasons beyond the carrier's control (e.g., weather), were not expected at departure to reach destination on time. The applicable rest tier is therefore driven by the *scheduled* duty period; operational delays do not retroactively convert a 10-hour rest day into a 12-hour rest day, but they also do not excuse shorting the rest actually given.
3. **No duty during rest.** The carrier may not assign a flight attendant to any duty with the carrier during a required rest period, and may not assign any duty period at all unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required (121.467(b)(10), (b)(11)).
4. **Rest means free of all restraint.** "Rest period" is defined as the period free of all restraint or duty and free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise (121.467(a)). On-call/standby arrangements that restrain the flight attendant do not count as rest.
5. **Travel is not rest.** Time spent in transportation, not local in character, that the carrier requires and provides to move the flight attendant to an airport where they will serve as a crewmember, or from an airport where they were relieved to return to their home station, is **not** part of the rest period (121.467(b)(12)). Long deadhead/positioning travel therefore must sit outside the 10 or 12 hours.
6. **Reduced rest must be paid back.** Where the 12-hour rest is reduced to 10, the subsequent rest must be at least 14 consecutive hours and must be *scheduled to begin* no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period (121.467(b)(8)). Track this as a rolling ledger; a reduced rest that is not followed by the 14-hour recovery within the 24-hour window is a violation even though the 10 hours themselves were given.
7. **Part 117 opt-in alternative.** Under 121.467(c), a carrier may instead apply the Part 117 flightcrew flight-time/duty/rest limits to its flight attendants for all operations under Part 121, provided it establishes the written procedures specified there. This is an all-operations election with procedural prerequisites, not a per-trip choice; where it is used, the Part 117 rest provisions govern instead of the 121.467(b) table above.

## 4. Worked examples (numbers checked against the table in §2)

- **Example A — short duty.** Scheduled duty 12:00–20:00 (8 hours, ≤14). Next duty may not be scheduled to begin before **06:00** the following day (10 consecutive hours). No reduction is available.
- **Example B — extended duty, full rest.** Scheduled duty of 16 hours with the additional flight attendant required by 121.467(b)(5), ending 22:00. Required rest is **12 consecutive hours**; next duty not before **10:00**.
- **Example C — extended duty, reduced rest with recovery.** Same 16-hour duty ending 22:00, carrier elects the (b)(8) reduction. Reduced rest of **10 hours** runs 22:00–08:00; next duty may start at 08:00. A subsequent rest of at least **14 consecutive hours** must then be scheduled to begin no later than **22:00 the following day** (24 hours after 22:00, the start of the reduced rest).
- **Example D — 24-in-7.** A flight attendant who has been on duty across six consecutive calendar days must be relieved from all further duty for at least **24 consecutive hours** within that 7-day span, independent of the daily 10-hour rests already given.

## 5. Reconciliation with the 9-hour / 8-hour figure seen in FAA material

The FAA's public FAQ page ("What are the flight attendant duty period and rest requirements?") states 9 consecutive hours, reducible to 8, with a following 10-hour rest. **That is not the Part 121 airline minimum.** Those figures are the text of 14 CFR 135.273(b)(2)–(3) (commuter/on-demand certificate holders) and 14 CFR 91.1062(a)(2)–(3) (program managers under management specifications). Part 121.467 sets 10 hours (not reducible) for duty periods of 14 hours or less and 12 hours for extended duty periods. Because the question is about a **US airline** — a Part 121 certificate holder conducting domestic, flag, or supplemental operations — the correct figure is **10 hours**. If the operation in question is actually a Part 135 commuter/on-demand carrier or a Part 91K fractional program, the answer changes to 9 hours (reducible to 8 with a 10-hour recovery); confirm the operating certificate before relying on either number.

## 6. What this figure is and is not

- It is the **federal regulatory floor** for Part 121 flight attendants. It is not a ceiling.
- Collective bargaining agreements and airline scheduling manuals routinely exceed it (e.g., 11–12 hours at home base, more on layover). Those provisions are enforceable contractually and must be checked separately; a schedule that meets 121.467 can still breach the CBA.
- State law and general employment-law rest rules are generally preempted as to airline duty/rest scheduling by the federal scheme, but this answer does not opine on any specific state statute; treat the federal rule as the operative scheduling floor.
- Pilot rest rules (Part 117) differ and do not govern flight attendants unless the carrier makes the 121.467(c) election described above.

## 7. Compliance verification checklist

For each pairing of consecutive duty periods, confirm:

1. Scheduled duty period length is recorded and the correct rest tier (10 or 12 hours) was applied.
2. Actual rest between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the next duty period is ≥ the required hours — no reduction below 10 under any circumstance.
3. Any 12→10 hour reduction is paired with a ≥14-hour subsequent rest scheduled to begin ≤24 hours after the reduced rest began.
4. Required non-local transportation time is excluded from the rest computation.
5. No duty of any kind is assigned or performed during the rest period; no restrained standby is counted as rest.
6. Every rolling 7-consecutive-calendar-day window contains ≥24 consecutive hours free from all further duty.
7. Any duty period over 14 hours carries documented compliance with the additional-flight-attendant conditions of 121.467(b)(4)–(b)(6).
8. If the carrier has elected the 121.467(c) Part 117 alternative, the written procedures exist and Part 117 limits are applied consistently across all Part 121 operations.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 10 on ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-i/subchapter-g/part-121/subpart-p/subject-group-ecfrb49759e744c709b/section-121.467 and 9 on ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-i/subchapter-f/part-91/subpart-k/subject-group-ecfrc17623c0e0be17e/section-91.1062. The first reads: "(2) A flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours."

question: H3
answer:
MAXIMUM WEIGHT FOR AN FAA 'SMALL UNMANNED AIRCRAFT' (SMALL UAS)

BOTTOM LINE
A drone counts as a 'small unmanned aircraft' / 'small UAS' under FAA rules only if it weighs LESS THAN 55 POUNDS on takeoff, including everything on board or otherwise attached to the aircraft.

- Threshold value: 55 lb
- Operative test: strictly less than 55 lb (a drone at exactly 55.00 lb does NOT qualify)
- Practical maximum: any takeoff weight below 55 lb, e.g. 54.99 lb (24.94 kg)
- Metric equivalent of the threshold: 55 lb = 24.9476 kg (24,947.6 g). The metric ceiling is therefore below 24.9476 kg. A 25 kg drone (55.12 lb) is NOT a small UAS.
- Weight basis: takeoff weight, fully configured — airframe + batteries + payload + cargo + any attached equipment

1. CONTROLLING REGULATION AND EXACT TEXT

14 CFR 107.3 (Definitions), Subpart A of Part 107:

  'Small unmanned aircraft means an unmanned aircraft weighing less than 55 pounds on takeoff, including everything that is on board or otherwise attached to the aircraft.'

  'Small unmanned aircraft system (small UAS) means a small unmanned aircraft and its associated elements (including communication links and the components that control the small unmanned aircraft) that are required for the safe and efficient operation of the small unmanned aircraft in the national airspace system.'

Citation history: Docket FAA-2015-0150, Amdt. 107-1, 81 FR 42209 (June 28, 2016), as amended by Amdt. 107-8, 86 FR 4381 (Jan. 15, 2021). Current text confirmed against eCFR (Title 14, Ch. I, Subch. F, Part 107, Subpart A, Sec. 107.3) and the 2026 GPO print of 14 CFR Ch. I.

Corroborating FAA statements:
- FAA, 'Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) Regulations (Part 107)': the rules cover 'drones weighing less than 55 pounds.'
- FAA, 'Operate a Drone, Start a Drone Program' (public safety): Part 107 allows operations of UAS 'under 55 pounds.'
- FAA FAQ, 'What are the requirements for operation of a UAS that weigh in excess of 55 pounds?': for civil operations with a UAS 'greater than 55 pounds,' you need an exemption under the Special Authority for Certain Unmanned Aircraft Systems, 49 U.S.C. 44807.

2. HOW TO APPLY THE TEST (COMPLIANCE INTERPRETATION)

(a) Strict inequality. The rule says 'less than 55 pounds,' not '55 pounds or less.' 55.00 lb is outside the definition. Design and document to a value below 55 lb, not at it. Recommended compliance margin for design/certification purposes: target a maximum takeoff weight of 54.5 lb (24.72 kg) or lower so that scale tolerance, paint, tape, an added action camera, or a last-minute accessory swap cannot push a compliant aircraft over the line.

(b) Takeoff weight, not empty weight. The measurement point is the aircraft at the moment of takeoff, in the configuration it will actually fly. Do not weigh the bare airframe and then add payload on paper.

(c) 'Everything that is on board or otherwise attached.' Included in the 55 lb:
  - airframe and structure
  - propulsion (motors, ESCs, propellers)
  - batteries / fuel / energy source
  - avionics, flight controller, GPS, antennas mounted on the aircraft
  - cameras, gimbals, sensors, lights, speakers, LiDAR
  - landing gear, parachutes, recovery systems
  - any payload or cargo
  - any external load that is attached (see (d))
  - attachment hardware, brackets, straps, quick-release mounts, ballast
Not included in the 55 lb (these are part of the 'system' but not 'on board or attached to the aircraft'):
  - the ground control station / controller / tablet / handset
  - ground-based communication links and ground antennas
  - the visual observer's equipment
Note the two definitions are different: 'small unmanned aircraft' carries the 55 lb limit; 'small UAS' is the aircraft plus its associated elements. The weight limit attaches to the aircraft.

(d) External loads and cargo. FAA guidance for Part 107 operations states a drone may carry an external load if it is securely attached and does not adversely affect flight characteristics or controllability, and that property may be transported for compensation or hire within state boundaries provided the drone (including its attached systems), payload, and cargo weigh less than 55 pounds total (some exceptions apply to Hawaii and the District of Columbia). So payload and cargo are inside the same 55 lb budget — there is no separate payload allowance.

(e) Re-weigh after any configuration change. A change of battery pack, addition of a parachute, swapping a camera, or adding a delivery box all change the takeoff weight and must be re-verified against the limit.

3. UNIT CONVERSIONS (for requesters who think in metric)

  55 lb x 0.45359237 kg/lb = 24.94758035 kg
  55 lb = 24,947.58 g

  Practical statements:
  - A drone qualifies if its takeoff weight is below 24.9476 kg (below 24,947.6 g).
  - To stay safely inside, design to 24.5 kg (54.01 lb) or less.
  - 25 kg = 55.1157 lb -> NOT a small UAS. This is the most common metric round-number error: 25 kg looks like 'about 55 lb' but is over the line.

  Quick reference table:
    24.00 kg = 52.91 lb  -> qualifies
    24.50 kg = 54.01 lb  -> qualifies (with margin)
    24.90 kg = 54.90 lb  -> qualifies (thin margin)
    24.9476 kg = 55.00 lb -> does NOT qualify (boundary is exclusive)
    25.00 kg = 55.12 lb  -> does NOT qualify
    55.00 lb exactly     -> does NOT qualify
    54.99 lb             -> qualifies

4. WHAT HAPPENS ON EACH SIDE OF THE LINE

Below 55 lb on takeoff:
  - The aircraft is a small unmanned aircraft; Part 107 is available for commercial/governmental operations (remote pilot certificate, registration, Remote ID, operating limitations of 107.51, waiver process under 107.200/107.205).
  - Limited recreational operations under 49 U.S.C. 44809 are likewise framed around UAS under that weight.

At or above 55 lb on takeoff:
  - The aircraft is not a small UAS; Part 107 does not apply. For civil operations the operator must obtain an exemption under 49 U.S.C. 44807 (Special Authority for Certain Unmanned Aircraft Systems) or pursue standard airworthiness certification. Public aircraft operators may use a COA under 49 U.S.C. 40102(a)/40125.

5. RELATED BUT DISTINCT WEIGHT THRESHOLDS (do not confuse with the small-UAS definition)

  - 0.55 lb (250 g): the FAA registration threshold for recreational flyers — drones at or under this weight generally need not be registered for recreational flight. It is NOT the small-drone definition. Under Part 107 every aircraft must be registered regardless of weight.
  - 0.55 lb (250 g): the Category 1 limit in Part 107 Subpart D (operations over people). Category 1/2/3 are about operations over human beings, not about whether the aircraft is a 'small' drone; Categories 2 and 3 have no weight cap but carry design/operational conditions.
  - 55 lb: the single weight line that defines 'small unmanned aircraft.'
  These three numbers are independent rules. Only the 55 lb line answers 'how heavy can a drone be and still count as a small drone.'

6. VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (how to prove compliance for a given aircraft)

Step 1 — Define the configuration. Freeze the as-flown configuration: airframe P/N, battery P/N and quantity, payload/cargo, attached accessories, attachment hardware.

Step 2 — Weigh. Use a calibrated scale with resolution of at least 0.01 lb (5 g) and a capacity comfortably above 55 lb; calibration traceable to NIST or equivalent. Weigh the complete aircraft in takeoff configuration, including batteries, payload, cargo, and all attached equipment. Tare any cradle/sling used to hold the aircraft.

Step 3 — Record. Log date, scale ID and calibration due date, configuration list, and measured weight. Repeat at least three times and use the highest reading.

Step 4 — Compare against the limit with the strict inequality. Accept only if measured weight < 55.00 lb. If the measured weight is 54.5 lb or higher, treat as marginal: re-weigh, and either reduce configured weight or document a plan to do so before flight.

Step 5 — Control changes. Any configuration change (battery swap, added sensor, parachute install, cargo load) triggers a re-weigh before flight. Keep the weight statement with the aircraft's documentation and, where applicable, in the declaration-of-compliance / means-of-compliance records for Subpart D categories.

Step 6 — Re-check the rule at answer time. Part 107 has been amended (e.g., Amdt. 107-8, Jan. 15, 2021, adding Subpart D and Remote ID-related content), and FAA guidance pages are periodically refreshed. Confirm 107.3's 'less than 55 pounds' language in the current eCFR before relying on it in a certification or customer-facing document.

7. SCOPE NOTE
This answer assumes U.S. FAA jurisdiction, since the FAA was named. The 55 lb figure is the FAA's; other authorities (EASA, Transport Canada, CAA) use different thresholds and classes (e.g., EASA's 25 kg / 900 g / 4 kg class lines), and those are not interchangeable with the FAA's small-UAS definition. The answer addresses classification only; the operating rules that follow from a given weight (registration, Remote ID, 107.51 limits, over-people categories, waivers) are separate questions.

8. SOURCES
- 14 CFR 107.3, eCFR (Title 14, Ch. I, Subch. F, Part 107, Subpart A) — definition of 'small unmanned aircraft.'
- 14 CFR Parts 107, 2026 GPO print (CFR-2026-title14-vol2), Sec. 107.3, 107.51.
- FAA, 'Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) Regulations (Part 107)' newsroom page.
- FAA, 'Operate a Drone, Start a Drone Program' (public safety) page.
- FAA FAQ, 'What are the requirements for operation of a UAS that weigh in excess of 55 pounds?'

answer:
BASIC VFR WEATHER MINIMUMS — CLASS E AIRSPACE BELOW 10,000 FT MSL (FAA / 14 CFR 91.155)

ANSWER
  Flight visibility:      3 statute miles
  Distance from clouds:   500 feet below the cloud
                          1,000 feet above the cloud
                          2,000 feet horizontally from the cloud

GOVERNING SOURCE
  14 CFR 91.155(a), Basic VFR weather minimums, table row "Class E: Less than 10,000 feet MSL." Corroborated by FAA AIM TBL 3-1-1 (AIM 3-1-4) and FAA AIP ENR 1.4, TBL ENR 1.4-1, which reproduce the same row verbatim. Any of these three is a valid citation for a compliance document; cite 14 CFR 91.155(a) as the primary authority.

FULL TABLE ROW AS PUBLISHED
  Airspace: Class E
  Altitude band: Less than 10,000 feet MSL
  Flight visibility: 3 statute miles
  Distance from clouds: 500 feet below; 1,000 feet above; 2,000 feet horizontal

SCOPE AND APPLICABILITY NOTES (all required for a correct, defensible answer)

1. Day vs. night. 14 CFR 91.155 draws no day/night distinction for Class E. The 3 SM / 500-1,000-2,000 minimums apply identically day and night. (Day/night splits in 91.155 exist only for Class G at or below 1,200 ft AGL and for Class G above 1,200 ft AGL.)

2. Altitude within Class E. The break in Class E is at 10,000 ft MSL, not at 1,200 ft AGL. There is no separate "Class E below 1,200 AGL" minimum in the FAA table; the 1,200 ft AGL break belongs to Class G. So the answer above holds for all Class E from the surface (where a Class E surface area exists) up to but not including 10,000 ft MSL.

3. Contrast case, at or above 10,000 ft MSL in Class E (do not confuse with the answer): 5 statute miles visibility; 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 1 statute mile horizontal. The horizontal clearance changes unit (statute miles, not feet) and the below-cloud clearance doubles to 1,000 ft.

4. Class E is more restrictive than Class G and less restrictive than Class D. ## OSHA PEL and Action Level — Respirable Crystalline Silica, General Industry

### Direct answer

| Limit | Value | Averaging | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Permissible exposure limit (PEL)** | **50 µg/m³** (= 0.050 mg/m³) | 8-hour time-weighted average (TWA) | 29 CFR 1910.1053(c) |
| **Action level (AL)** | **25 µg/m³** (= 0.025 mg/m³) | 8-hour TWA | 29 CFR 1910.1053(b), definition of "Action level" |

Both are concentrations of **airborne respirable crystalline silica** — i.e., quartz, cristobalite, and/or tridymite in the respirable particle-size fraction as determined by a sampler meeting ISO 7708:1995 (29 CFR 1910.1053(b), definition of "Respirable crystalline silica").

### Verbatim regulatory text (as fetched from eCFR, 29 CFR 1910.1053)

- §1910.1053(b): "**Action level** means a concentration of airborne respirable crystalline silica of 25 µg/m3, calculated as an 8-hour TWA."
- §1910.1053(c): "**Permissible exposure limit (PEL).** The employer shall ensure that no employee is exposed to an airborne concentration of respirable crystalline silica in excess of 50 µg/m3, calculated as an 8-hour TWA."

The same two figures appear identically in the 2016 and 2018 printed CFR volumes (GovInfo PDFs of 29 CFR 1910.1053), confirming these are the values as promulgated in the 2016 silica rulemaking and unchanged in the current eCFR text.

### Definitions that govern how the numbers are applied

- **Employee exposure** — "the exposure to airborne crystalline silica that would occur if the employee were not using a respirator" (§1910.1053(b)). Compliance is judged on the *unprotected* exposure; respirators do not change the measured exposure for PEL/AL comparison, they only supplement controls.
- **8-hour TWA** — the standard's averaging basis regardless of actual shift length. For shifts longer than 8 hours, the measured exposure must be converted to an 8-hour TWA before comparison with 50 or 25 µg/m³. (Shift-length conversion method is a separate technical question; the standard states the limits only on an 8-hour TWA basis.)

### What each number triggers (why both must be reported)

| Concentration (8-hr TWA) | Regulatory consequence | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| Below 25 µg/m³ (AL) | No exposure assessment or periodic monitoring obligation for those employees; employer may discontinue monitoring for employees represented by such results | 1910.1053(d)(3)(ii), (d)(3)(v) |
| At or above 25 µg/m³ (AL) | Exposure assessment required; periodic monitoring at least every 6 months while at/above AL but at/below PEL | 1910.1053(d)(1), (d)(3)(iii) |
| At or above 25 µg/m³ (AL) for **30 or more days per year** | Medical surveillance must be offered | 1910.1053(i)(1)(i) |
| Above 50 µg/m³ (PEL) | Engineering and work practice controls required (unless infeasible), supplemented by respiratory protection; monitoring repeated at least every 3 months; written exposure control plan required | 1910.1053(e), (f), (g), (d)(3)(iv) |
| Any exposure, if a written exposure control plan is required | Plan must describe tasks, controls, and housekeeping | 1910.1053(f)(2) |

### Scope notes specific to "general industry"

- The general industry standard is **29 CFR 1910.1053**. Construction is a separate standard (**29 CFR 1926.1153**) with a Table 1 task-based compliance option and its own AL of 25 µg/m³ and PEL of 50 µg/m³; shipyards/maritime are addressed under 29 CFR 1915. Do not cite 1926.1153 values as general industry authority, even though the numeric limits coincide.
- §1910.1053(a)(2)–(3) contains two narrow carve-outs: the section does not apply (i) where the employer has **objective data** demonstrating exposure will remain **below 25 µg/m³** as an 8-hour TWA under any foreseeable conditions, or (ii) where the employer complies with 1926.1153 and the task is indistinguishable from a Table 1 construction task and is not performed regularly in the same environment and conditions. Note the first carve-out uses the same 25 µg/m³ figure as the action level.
- Sampling/analytical methods for demonstrating compliance are given in **Appendix A to 1910.1053** (e.g., XRD or IR methods for respirable quartz/cristobalite/tridymite); the PEL/AL are performance limits, not method limits.

### Unit conventions (a frequent source of error)

Silica limits are conventionally stated in **µg/m³**, unlike most OSHA PELs which are in mg/m³. Conversions: 50 µg/m³ = 0.050 mg/m³; 25 µg/m³ = 0.025 mg/m³. If a program document states "0.05 mg/m³," confirm it is on an 8-hour TWA respirable basis and is not a mis-transcription of the ACGIH TLV (see below).

### Do not conflate with other bodies' limits (outside the ask; verify before citing)

- **NIOSH REL**: 0.05 mg/m³ (50 µg/m³) respirable crystalline silica, TWA for up to a 10-hour workday/40-hour week — numerically equal to the OSHA PEL but a *recommended*, not enforceable, limit with a different averaging basis.
- **ACGIH TLV**: respirable quartz on the order of 0.025 mg/m³ (25 µg/m³) — numerically equal to the OSHA *action level*, not the PEL. Citing this as "the OSHA PEL" is the most common downstream error.
- **MSHA**: separate metal/nonmetal and coal standards with their own respirable quartz/dust limits; not applicable to general industry under OSHA jurisdiction.

(These comparison values are provided only to prevent misattribution; they are not part of the requested answer and their current editions should be confirmed against the issuing body's own publication before use.)

### Point-in-time caveat

Values above reflect the current eCFR text of 29 CFR 1910.1053 as fetched (2026-11-17) and match the 2016 and 2018 CFR printings. The rule's compliance dates were staggered (most obligations within 90 days of the 2016 promulgation; medical surveillance and engineering-control obligations phased in over subsequent years for general industry). If you are assessing historical compliance or a pre-effective-date condition, confirm which provisions were in force on the date in question; the numeric PEL and AL themselves have not changed since promulgation.

In the 1876 first edition of Robert's Rules of Order (the Pocket Manual of Rules of Order for Deliberative Assemblies), a motion for the Previous Question requires a TWO-THIRDS VOTE (2/3) to be adopted. A bare majority is not sufficient. The manual classes the Previous Question with the motions that take away the right of debate, and it attaches the two-thirds threshold to it for that reason.

WHAT THE RULE PROVIDES (substance; see the verification procedure below for lifting the verbatim sentence)

1. The Previous Question is a privileged motion whose object is to close debate and bring the assembly to an immediate vote on the pending question.

# Luminous efficacy Kcd in the SI Brochure, 9th edition (2019)

## Direct answers

| Quantity | Fixed value | Unit | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 x 10^12 Hz, Kcd | **683** | lm W^-1 (= cd sr W^-1 = cd sr kg^-1 m^-2 s^3) | exact, by definition; no uncertainty |
| Frequency of the monochromatic radiation to which that value applies | **540 x 10^12 Hz** (= 540 THz = 5.4 x 10^14 Hz = 540 000 000 000 000 Hz) | Hz (= s^-1) | exact, specified value; no uncertainty |

Kcd = 683 lm/W exactly, for monochromatic radiation of frequency exactly 540 x 10^12 Hz.

## Definition as given in the 9th edition

SI Brochure, 9th edition (2019), Table 1 (The seven base units of the SI), entry for luminous intensity:

> "The candela, symbol cd, is the SI unit of luminous intensity in a given direction. It is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 x 10^12 Hz, Kcd, to be 683 when expressed in the unit lm W^-1, which is equal to cd sr W^-1, or cd sr kg^-1 m^-2 s^3, where the kilogram, metre and second are defined in terms of h, c and ΔνCs."

The same edition states the constant in its list of the seven defining constants:

> "the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 x 10^12 Hz, Kcd, is 683 lm/W"

with the unit relations spelled out in the same passage: "Hz = s^-1, J = kg m^2 s^-2, C = A s, lm = cd sr, and W = kg m^2 s^-3".

Appendix 2 to the 9th edition (Appendix 2 v1.02, 22 March 2021), section 2 "Definition of the candela", restates it identically:

> "The candela, symbol cd, is the SI unit of luminous intensity in a given direction. It is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 x 10^12 Hz, Kcd, to be 683 when expressed in the unit lm W^-1, which is equal to cd sr W^-1, or cd sr kg^-1 m^-2 s^3, where the kilogram, metre and second are defined in terms of h, c and ΔνCs."

## Exactness and uncertainty

Both numbers are **exact and carry no uncertainty**. The 9th edition is explicit about the mechanism: "These definitions specify the exact numerical value of each constant when its value is expressed in the corresponding SI unit. By fixing the exact numerical value, the unit becomes defined, since the product of the numerical value and the unit has to equal the value of the constant, which is invariant." Kcd is one of the seven defining constants of the revised SI; 683 is a fixed numerical value, not a measured result, so it must not be quoted with a +/- or a significant-figure caveat, and it must not be rounded or converted (e.g. it is not "about 683" and not "683.0").

The implied exact relation, as written in the draft text of the 9th edition, is:

> "This definition implies the exact relation Kcd = 683 cd sr kg^-1 m^-2 s^3 for monochromatic radiation of frequency ν = 540 x 10^12 Hz."

## Frequency vs. wavelength — important framing

The defining condition is stated as a **frequency**, not a wavelength: ν = 540 x 10^12 Hz. This has been the case since the 1979 (16th CGPM) definition of the candela; the wavelength-based formulation (555 nm) belongs to the earlier 1948/1967 definition. So the frequency form should not be described as new to the 2019 revision.

Appendix 2 does give a wavelength, but only as a derived annotation for practical photometry, not as the definition:

> "where fa = 555.017 nm is the wavelength in standard air at the frequency of 540 x 10^12 Hz given in the definition of Kcd"

If this is quoted, it must be labelled as a derived, approximate convenience value in standard air (dependent on the refractive index of air), never as the defining condition and never as an exact defined constant.

## Revision consistency (2018 draft vs. 2019 published text vs. Appendix 2 v1.02)

The three texts consulted agree on both numbers, so there is no revision-dependent discrepancy to resolve for this question:

- Draft of the ninth SI Brochure, 5 February 2018: "...frequency 540 x 10^12 Hz, Kcd, to be 683 when expressed in the unit lm W^-1..."
- SI Brochure 9th edition (2019), Table 1 and the defining-constants list: "...frequency 540 x 10^12 Hz, Kcd, to be 683..." / "...is 683 lm/W".
- SI Brochure 9th edition (2019), Appendix 2 v1.02, 22 March 2021: identical definition.

For citation purposes, quote the 2019 published 9th edition (Table 1, and the defining-constants list in the Introduction), and cite Appendix 2 v1.02 (22 March 2021) if a section-level reference for the candela is wanted.

## Physical meaning (optional context, if the surrounding definition is wanted)

Per the draft text of the 9th edition: "The effect of this definition is that one candela is the luminous intensity, in a given direction, of a source that emits monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 x 10^12 Hz and has a radiant intensity in that direction of (1/683) W/sr." Appendix 2 adds that the definition "is expressed in strictly physical terms and is given for only one frequency of the electromagnetic radiation"; for practical sources emitting at other frequencies, photometric quantities are obtained by weighting the spectral power distribution with the CIE spectral luminous efficiency function V(λ) and scaling by Kcd. The older language about "photopic vision" and the blackbody at the freezing point of platinum is superseded and should not be attached to this definition.

## Common errors to avoid

- Writing 683 lm/W with an uncertainty or as a measured value.
- Writing 540 x 10^12 Hz as "540 Hz", "540 THz +/- ...", or converting to a rounded wavelength and calling that the definition.
- Confusing Kcd (683 lm/W) with the maximum luminous efficacy of the eye (~683 lm/W at 555 nm) as a physiological limit — in the SI it is a defined constant, not a measured biological maximum.
- Using "cd sr kg^-1 m^-2 s^3" without noting it is the same unit as lm W^-1.

## Source

BIPM, Le Systeme international d'unites (SI Brochure), 9th edition, 2019 — Table 1 and the list of seven defining constants; and Appendix 2 (SI Brochure 9th edition, Appendix 2 v1.02, 22 March 2021), section 2.
