REGULATORY DETERMINATION — 49 CFR CLASSIFICATION OF A LIQUID WITH FLASH POINT 65 °C

1. ANSWER
No. A liquid with a flash point of 65 °C that meets the definition of no other hazard class is NOT a Class 3 flammable liquid under the US Hazardous Materials Regulations. It is a COMBUSTIBLE LIQUID as defined in 49 CFR 173.120(b)(1).

2. GOVERNING TEXT (49 CFR, current edition — eCFR text current as of 2025-10-01; the 60 °C threshold has been stable for decades, so the answer is not edition-sensitive)

§ 173.120(a) — Flammable liquid: "a flammable liquid (Class 3) means a liquid having a flash point of not more than 60 °C (140 °F), or any material in a liquid phase with a flash point at or above 37.8 °C (100 °F) that is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging, with the following exceptions: ..."

§ 173.120(b)(1) — Combustible liquid: "a combustible liquid means any liquid that does not meet the definition of any other hazard class specified in this subchapter and has a flash point above 60 °C (140 °F) and below 93 °C (200 °F)."

3. DECISION PATH
Step 1 — Compare against the Class 3 ceiling. 65 °C vs. 60 °C (140 °F). 65 > 60, margin 5 °C (9 °F). The first limb of 173.120(a) fails.
Step 2 — Test the elevated-temperature limb of 173.120(a). That limb captures a liquid with flash point ≥ 37.8 °C (100 °F) only if it is (i) intentionally heated AND (ii) offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point AND (iii) in a bulk packaging. 65 °C satisfies the temperature screen, but the material is assumed to be offered at ambient temperature, i.e. not intentionally heated and not at/above 65 °C. Limb fails. (See § 6 for the flip condition.)
Step 3 — Apply the 173.120(a)(1)–(5) exceptions. They are exceptions FROM Class 3 (liquids meeting the § 173.115 flammable-gas definitions; mixtures ≥99% volume of components with FP ≥ 60 °C not shipped at/above flash point; liquids with FP > 35 °C that do not sustain combustion per ASTM D 4206 / Part 173 Appendix H; FP > 35 °C with fire point > 100 °C per ISO 2592; FP > 35 °C water-miscible solutions with > 90% water). They are not needed to reach the verdict — the material already fails the 60 °C ceiling — and none of them can pull a material INTO Class 3. No effect on the outcome.
Step 4 — Apply 173.120(b)(1). Does it meet any other hazard class? No (given, and stated as a verified premise, not presumed). Is the flash point above 60 °C? Yes (65). Is it below 93 °C? Yes (65 < 93). Both bounds satisfied strictly; the material is a combustible liquid.
Step 5 — Check 173.120(b)(2) / 173.150(f)(1). This provision lets "a flammable liquid with a flash point at or above 38 °C (100 °F)" be RECLASSED as a combustible liquid. It does not apply here: reclassing presupposes a material that is Class 3 in the first place. This liquid is combustible by definition. Consequence: the restriction in those paragraphs ("does not apply to transportation by vessel or aircraft, except where other means of transportation is impracticable") does not restrict this material. The definitional classification holds for all modes under the HMR.

4. TEMPERATURE CONVERSIONS USED (all consistent with the values above)
°F = °C × 9/5 + 32
- 60 °C = 140 °F (Class 3 ceiling; 173.120(a))
- 65 °C = 149 °F (subject liquid)
- 93 °C = 199.4 °F ≈ 200 °F (combustible-liquid upper bound; 173.120(b)(1))
- 37.8 °C = 100.0 °F (elevated-temperature screen; 173.120(a))
Subject liquid at 149 °F: 9 °F above the 140 °F Class 3 ceiling, 51 °F below the 200 °F combustible-liquid ceiling. No stated value crosses a stated bound.

5. WHAT THE CLASSIFICATION MEANS OPERATIONALLY (§ 173.150(f))
A combustible liquid is not one of the nine HMR hazard classes; "combustible liquid" is a defined term, not a class. It is therefore generally not a hazardous material for HMR purposes unless it independently triggers another basis for regulation.
- Non-bulk packaging: § 173.150(f)(2) — "The requirements in this subchapter do not apply to a material classed as a combustible liquid in a non-bulk packaging unless the combustible liquid is a hazardous substance, a hazardous waste, or a marine pollutant." So: no shipping paper, no Class 3 label, no placards, no specification packaging, no 172.101 Table entry, no hazmat employee training driven by Class 3 — provided the material is none of those three.
- Bulk packaging, or hazardous substance / hazardous waste / marine pollutant: § 173.150(f)(3) — the HMR do not apply except for the enumerated items, which begin with (i) shipping papers, waybills, switching orders, and hazardous waste manifests and (ii) marking of packages, and continue through the remainder of (f)(3) (placarding, emergency response information, incident reporting, and training, as listed in the full paragraph). Read § 173.150(f)(3)(i)–(viii) in full before writing the shipping paper.
- Escape hatch: § 173.120(b)(3) — "A combustible liquid that does not sustain combustion is not subject to the requirements of this subchapter as a combustible liquid," testable by ASTM D 4206 or Part 173 Appendix H. If a sustain-combustion test is run and the material does not sustain combustion, even the limited bulk requirements of 173.150(f)(3) fall away. This is optional, not required.
- Hazardous substance screen: verify against 40 CFR 302 Table 302.4 (CERCLA) and the § 172.101 Appendix A list; a reportable quantity designation changes the answer in § 5 above regardless of the combustible-liquid status. Same for marine pollutant (§ 172.101 Appendix B) and hazardous waste (40 CFR 261).

6. CONDITIONS THAT WOULD FLIP THE VERDICT TO CLASS 3
(a) Intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above 65 °C in a bulk packaging → Class 3 under the second limb of 173.120(a). Note § 173.120(b)(2) expressly forecloses reclassing such an elevated-temperature material as a combustible liquid.
(b) Flash point re-determined at ≤ 60 °C (≤ 140 °F) by an accepted method under § 173.120(c). The 65 °C figure is only as good as its test method: § 173.120(c) requires the flash point to be determined by a specified procedure — for a homogeneous, single-phase liquid of viscosity < 45 S.U.S. at 38 °C that does not form a surface film, ASTM D 56 (Tag closed cup), D 3278, or D 3828 (small-scale closed cup). An open-cup result (e.g. Cleveland open cup) is not the regulatory basis for this classification and typically reads higher than closed cup; a 65 °C open-cup value could correspond to a closed-cup value at or below 60 °C. Confirm the method and the reported closed-cup result before relying on this determination.
(c) The liquid is later found to meet another hazard class (e.g. Class 8 corrosivity, Class 6.1 toxicity, Class 9) → it is regulated on that basis and the 173.120(b)(1) combustible-liquid definition is unavailable by its own terms ("does not meet the definition of any other hazard class").
(d) The material is a hazardous substance, hazardous waste, or marine pollutant → HMR apply notwithstanding combustible-liquid status.

7. DOCUMENTATION RECOMMENDED
Retain in the shipping file: (i) the flash point test report showing the closed-cup method (ASTM D 56 / D 3278 / D 3828) and the 65 °C result; (ii) the basis for the "no other hazard class" determination (SDS review, pH/corrosivity, toxicity, reactivity, environmental screening); (iii) the CERCLA/marine-pollutant/hazardous-waste screens; (iv) the packaging configuration (non-bulk vs. bulk); (v) this determination, signed and dated, citing 49 CFR 173.120(a) and (b)(1) and 173.150(f).

8. SCOPE NOTE
The verdict above is a 49 CFR (domestic US DOT) determination. For air, the ICAO Technical Instructions / IATA DGR use the same 60 °C closed-cup cutoff for Class 3, so the material is likewise not a Class 3 dangerous good there, but some carriers apply their own combustible-liquid acceptance rules; for vessel, the IMDG Code Class 3 cutoff is also 60 °C. Those regimes were not researched here and are outside this determination — confirm with the carrier or the applicable modal regime before tendering the material for international movement.

question: H17
answer:
ANSWER — NRC dose limits for individual members of the public (10 CFR Part 20, Subpart D, as currently in effect; values unchanged since the 1991 revision, 56 FR 23398, May 21, 1991)

TABLE 1 — The two limits requested

| # | Limit | Dose quantity | Pathway / where it applies | Citation |
|---|-------|---------------|----------------------------|----------|
| 1 | 0.1 rem (1 mSv) per year | Total effective dose equivalent (TEDE) | All exposure from the licensed operation — external + internal, all pathways | 10 CFR 20.1301(a)(1) |
| 2 | 0.002 rem (0.02 mSv) in any one hour | Dose (dose rate over a one-hour period) | External sources only, in any unrestricted area | 10 CFR 20.1301(a)(2) |

So: per year the limit is 0.1 rem (1 mSv) TEDE; in any one hour in an unrestricted area the limit is 0.002 rem (0.02 mSv) from external sources.

---

1. THE ANNUAL LIMIT — 20.1301(a)(1)

Verbatim: "Each licensee shall conduct operations so that— (1) The total effective dose equivalent to individual members of the public from the licensed operation does not exceed 0.1 rem (1 mSv) in a year, exclusive of the dose contributions from background radiation, from any medical administration the individual has received, from exposure to individuals administered radioactive material and released under 35.75, from voluntary participation in medical research programs, and from the licensee's disposal of radioactive material into sanitary sewerage in accordance with 20.2003."

- Quantity: TEDE, i.e., the sum of the deep-dose equivalent from external exposure plus the committed effective dose equivalent from internal intake (20.1202 summation method applied to the public).
- Scope: "from the licensed operation" — both effluent releases (gaseous and liquid) and direct radiation.
- Excluded from the 0.1 rem count (do not subtract them from measured dose; they are simply outside the limit): natural background; the individual's own medical administration; exposure to patients released under 35.75; voluntary participation in medical research; and the licensee's sanitary-sewerage disposal under 20.2003.

2. THE HOURLY LIMIT — 20.1301(a)(2)

Verbatim: "(2) The dose in any unrestricted area from external sources, exclusive of the dose contributions from patients administered radioactive material and released in accordance with 35.75, does not exceed 0.002 rem (0.02 millisievert) in any one hour."

- Quantity: dose in one hour — i.e., a dose-rate limit, 0.002 rem/h (20 microSv/h), evaluated for the highest one-hour period, not an annual accumulation.
- Pathway: external sources only. There is no per-hour internal/effluent counterpart in Part 20; airborne and liquid effluent compliance is governed by the annual limit and by Appendix B Table 2 concentrations (see 20.1302(b)(2)(i)).
- Location: any unrestricted area. "Unrestricted area" (20.1003) = an area to which access is neither limited by the licensee for purposes of protection of individuals from exposure to radiation and radioactive materials, nor any area used for residential quarters.
- It is an area-based limit, so it applies whether or not a member of the public happens to be standing there at that moment.

CRITICAL: THE TWO LIMITS ARE CONCURRENT AND INDEPENDENT. The hourly value is not an annual budget and must not be integrated. 0.002 rem/h x 8,760 h = 17.52 rem/y — that figure is not a permissible annual dose; it is shown only to demonstrate why the hourly limit cannot be annualized. A licensee must satisfy 20.1301(a)(1) and (a)(2) simultaneously; the annual limit is the binding constraint on sustained exposure, and the hourly limit caps short-term peaks.

3. HOW COMPLIANCE IS DEMONSTRATED — 20.1302

- 20.1302(a): licensee must survey radiation levels in unrestricted and controlled areas, and radioactive material in effluents, to demonstrate compliance with 20.1301.
- 20.1302(b)(1): demonstrate by measurement or calculation that the TEDE to the individual likely to receive the highest dose (the maximally exposed member of the public) does not exceed the annual limit; OR
- 20.1302(b)(2): demonstrate that (i) annual average effluent concentrations at the unrestricted-area boundary do not exceed Appendix B Table 2 values, AND (ii) if an individual were continuously present in an unrestricted area, the dose from external sources would not exceed 0.002 rem (0.02 mSv) in an hour and 0.05 rem (0.5 mSv) in a year.
- Note on internal consistency: the 0.05 rem/y external-source screening value in 20.1302(b)(2)(ii) is more restrictive than the 0.1 rem/y TEDE limit because it covers only the external pathway; a licensee meeting the screening value is conservative with respect to 20.1301(a)(1).
- If the licensee permits members of the public access to controlled areas, the public limits continue to apply to those individuals (20.1301(b)).

4. RELATED PROVISIONS THAT MODIFY OR TIGHTEN THE LIMITS

- 20.1301(c): a conditional allowance, quoted in part — "...ation dose greater than 0.1 rem (1 mSv) if— (1) The radiation dose received does not exceed 0.5 rem (5 mSv); and (2) The authorized user, as defined in 10 CFR Part 35, has determined before the visit that it is appropriate." (Quoted from the regulation; the paragraph conditions an above-0.1-rem dose on a 0.5 rem (5 mSv) cap plus a prior authorized-user determination.)
- 20.1301(d): a licensee or license applicant may apply for prior NRC authorization to operate up to an annual public dose limit of 0.5 rem (5 mSv), showing need and duration, an assessment/control program, and ALARA procedures. Absent such authorization, 0.1 rem/y governs.
- 20.1301(e): a licensee subject to EPA's generally applicable environmental radiation standards (40 CFR Part 190) must also comply with those standards. For the uranium fuel cycle those are 25 mrem/y whole body, 75 mrem/y thyroid, 25 mrem/y any other organ — more restrictive than 0.1 rem/y and therefore controlling in practice for those licensees. Separately, 40 CFR Part 61 Subpart I (NESHAP, radionuclide air emissions) imposes a 10 mrem/y EDEdose constraint on major emitters.
- 20.1301(f): the Commission may impose additional restrictions on radiation levels in unrestricted areas and on total radionuclide quantities released, to restrict collective dose.
- ALARA: 20.1101(b) requires doses to be as low as reasonably achievable; Appendix I to Part 20 supplies numerical guidance (dose design objectives for effluent releases) that is well below the 20.1301 limits. ALARA and the EPA/40 CFR 61 constraints, not 20.1301, are typically the operative design targets.

5. DEFINITIONS THAT BOUND THE ANSWER (20.1003)

- Member of the public: any individual except when that individual is receiving an occupational dose. A worker is not a member of the public while occupationally exposed; a visitor, neighbor, or non-occupationally exposed employee is.
- Unrestricted area: see section 2 above.
- Total effective dose equivalent: deep-dose equivalent (external) + committed effective dose equivalent (internal).

6. UNIT CONVERSIONS USED THROUGHOUT (1 rem = 10 mSv)

| rem | mSv | Where it appears |
|-----|-----|------------------|
| 0.002 rem/h | 0.02 mSv/h (20 microSv/h) | 20.1301(a)(2) — hourly, external, unrestricted area |
| 0.05 rem/y | 0.5 mSv/y | 20.1302(b)(2)(ii) — external-source screening value |
| 0.1 rem/y | 1 mSv/y | 20.1301(a)(1) — annual TEDE |
| 0.5 rem | 5 mSv | 20.1301(c), (d) — conditional/authorized allowances |

7. VALUES THAT ARE NOT THE ANSWER (named to prevent misapplication)

- 2 mrem in any one hour / 100 mrem in any 7 consecutive days / 500 mrem in a year: the pre-1991 rule (former 10 CFR 20.105(b)) for unrestricted areas. Superseded; do not use under the current Part 20.
- 5 rem (50 mSv) per year: the adult occupational limit, 20.1201(a)(1) — applies to occupationally exposed adults, not members of the public.
- 0.5 rem (5 mSv) over the entire pregnancy: the embryo/fetus limit for a declared pregnant worker, 20.1208 — occupational, not public.
- 100 mrem/y: frequently cited from DOE Order 458.1 / EPA guidance, not from 10 CFR 20.1301.

8. JURISDICTIONAL NOTE

The above are the NRC's values. NRC licensees in Agreement States are regulated under the state's adopted, NRC-compatible rules; the values are normally identical to 20.1301 because compatibility is required, but a state may be more restrictive, and the state citation rather than 10 CFR 20.1301 would then be the operative authority. For an NRC-jurisdiction licensee the citations above are the answer.

9. CITATION BASIS AND EDITION CONTROL

- 10 CFR 20.1301 and 20.1302 as set out in the current eCFR (fetched 2026-11-17) and the 2025 print (10 CFR Ch. I, 1-1-25 Edition) and 2024 print; the text of 20.1301 is identical in the 2016, 2024, and 2025 editions and in the current eCFR, so the answer is edition-insensitive.
- Source note for Subpart D: 56 FR 23398, May 21, 1991, as amended (amendments to the surrounding sections include 60 FR 48625, Sept. 20, 1995; 62 FR 4133, Jan. 29, 1997; 67 FR 20370, Apr. 24, 2002; 67 FR 62872, Oct. 9, 2002 — these updated cross-references, principally to 35.75, not the numeric limits).

This is a statement of the regulatory limits as published; it is not legal advice and does not analyze any specific licensee's compliance.

question: H2
answer:
COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION — ALCOHOL CONCENTRATION BAR FOR US CMV DRIVERS

1. ANSWER
A driver of a commercial motor vehicle in the United States is barred from performing safety-sensitive functions at an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater. The threshold is inclusive: exactly 0.04 is a violation; 0.039 is not a violation of the concentration prohibition (though other prohibitions and consequences may still apply — see §4).

Regulatory basis: 49 CFR §382.201 (FMCSA; Title 49, Subtitle B, Chapter III, Subchapter B, Part 382 'Controlled Substances and Alcohol Use and Testing', Subpart B 'Prohibitions').

2. CONTROLLING TEXT — 49 CFR §382.201 'Alcohol concentration'
'No driver shall report for duty or remain on duty requiring the performance of safety-sensitive functions while having an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater. No employer having knowledge that a driver has an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater shall permit the driver to perform or continue to perform safety-sensitive functions.' [66 FR 43103, Aug. 17, 2001, as amended at 77 FR 4483, Jan. 30, 2012]

Drafting note for anyone quoting this: the second sentence in the current text reads 'having knowledge'. Older CFR snapshots (e.g., the 2006 and 2010 volumes) read 'having actual knowledge'; the 2012 amendment (77 FR 4483) removed 'actual'. Quote the current text.

3. UNITS AND MEASUREMENT
- 'Alcohol concentration' is defined in §382.107 as the concentration of alcohol in a person's blood or breath, expressed as grams of alcohol per 210 liters of breath or grams per 100 milliliters of blood. 0.04 therefore means 0.04 g/210 L breath (BrAC) or 0.04 g/100 mL blood (BAC).
- DOT alcohol testing under 49 CFR Part 40 is performed with an evidential breath testing device (EBT); blood is not an authorized specimen for a DOT alcohol test. In practice the operative number on a DOT test is a breath result of 0.04 g/210 L.
- The 0.04 determination is made on the confirmation test, not the screening test. Under Part 40 Subpart C, a screening result below 0.02 is negative; a screening result of 0.02 or greater must be followed by a confirmation test (see §40.251 screening procedure and §40.253 confirmation procedure), and the confirmation test result is the result of record. A screening result alone cannot establish a §382.201 violation.

4. THE THRESHOLD LADDER — DO NOT CONFLATE THE 0.02 AND 0.04 FIGURES
| Confirmation test result | Regulatory effect | Citation |
| below 0.02 | Negative test. No Part 382 alcohol violation on concentration grounds. | Part 40 Subpart C (§40.251) |
| 0.02 to 0.039 | Not a §382.201 violation, but the driver may not perform safety-sensitive functions (including driving a CMV) until the start of the next regularly scheduled duty period, and not less than 24 hours after the test was administered. | §382.505(a) |
| 0.04 or greater | Violation. Driver may not report for or remain on duty in a safety-sensitive function; employer may not permit performance; removal and return-to-duty process required. | §382.201; §382.501; §382.503 |
| Refusal to submit to a required alcohol test | Treated as a violation; driver barred from safety-sensitive functions. | §382.211; §40.191 |
| Return-to-duty eligibility | Requires a return-to-duty alcohol test result of less than 0.02. | §382.309(a) |
Note also §382.505(b): an employer may not take action under Part 382 against a driver based solely on a result below 0.04, but this does not restrict action taken under independent authority (e.g., company policy, state law, collective bargaining agreement) consistent with law.

5. NON-CONCENTRATION PROHIBITIONS THAT BAR DUTY AT ANY LEVEL
A driver can be barred from safety-sensitive duty with an alcohol concentration below 0.04 — including 0.00 on a test — because Part 382 separately prohibits conduct, not just concentration:
- §382.205 On-duty use: no alcohol while performing safety-sensitive functions.
- §382.207 Pre-duty use: no safety-sensitive functions within four hours after using alcohol.
- §382.209 Use following an accident: no alcohol for eight hours following an accident requiring a post-accident test, or until the post-accident alcohol test is administered, whichever occurs first.
- §382.211 Refusal to submit to a required test.
- §382.213/§382.215 (controlled substances) — separate from alcohol.
These are conduct/time prohibitions; they are not concentration thresholds and should not be quoted as such.

6. EMPLOYER OBLIGATIONS ON A CONFIRMATION RESULT OF 0.04 OR GREATER
1. Immediate removal. The driver must be removed from safety-sensitive functions, including driving a CMV, and must not be permitted to perform them (§382.201, second sentence; §382.501(a)–(b)).
2. Clearinghouse reporting. The employer reports the alcohol violation to the FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse under Part 382 Subpart G (§382.705), and the driver is subject to the query/consent and reporting provisions of §§382.701–382.711.
3. Evaluation and referral. Before any return to safety-sensitive duty, the driver must be evaluated by a Substance Abuse Professional and complete the education/treatment referral and SAP re-evaluation (§382.503; §382.605).
4. Return-to-duty and follow-up testing. The driver must pass a return-to-duty alcohol test with a result below 0.02 (§382.309(a)) and is subject to a follow-up testing plan (§382.311).
5. Records. Alcohol test results indicating a concentration of 0.02 or greater are retained for five years (§382.401), included in the annual summary of test results (§382.403), and accessible to the driver and to authorized officials (§382.405).
6. Policy and training. The employer's written policy (§382.601) and supervisor training for reasonable-suspicion determinations (§382.603) must reflect the 0.04 bar.

7. COMPANION FMCSA PROVISIONS AT THE SAME 0.04 FIGURE (consistency check)
The 0.04 number is uniform across the FMCSA alcohol rules, so the answer does not depend on which provision is cited:
- §392.5(a): no driver may operate a CMV with an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater (with a 24-hour stand-down for 0.02–0.039).
- §383.51: driving a CMV with a BAC of 0.04 or greater is a major offense carrying CDL disqualification.
- Part 382 §382.201: the safety-sensitive-duty bar (the provision that answers this question).

8. SCOPE LIMITS AND COMMON MIS-ANSWERS
- 0.08 is the typical state per-se DUI threshold for non-commercial drivers; it is not the federal CMV safety-sensitive-duty bar. The federal CMV bar is lower.
- There is no federal 'zero tolerance' concentration threshold in Part 382. A result below 0.02 is a negative test, subject to the conduct prohibitions in §5 and the 24-hour rule at 0.02–0.039.
- Other DOT modes set their own thresholds and are not authority for a CMV driver: FTA (49 CFR 655.35) bars covered transit employees at 0.02; FAA (14 CFR 91.17), FRA (49 CFR 219.101), USCG and PHMSA use 0.04. This determination is FMCSA-specific.
- State law may impose additional or different requirements; it does not displace §382.201 for drivers subject to Part 382.
- A blood test result from a hospital or law enforcement is not a DOT alcohol test and cannot by itself establish a §382.201 violation; the DOT determination rests on the Part 40 EBT confirmation result.

9. SOURCES CONSULTED
- eCFR, 49 CFR §382.201 (current): https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-III/subchapter-B/part-382/subpart-B/section-382.201
- eCFR, 49 CFR Part 382 (current, incl. §§382.205, 382.207, 382.209, 382.501, 382.505): https://ecfr.gov/current/title-49/part-382
- GovInfo, CFR 2025 Title 49 Vol. 5, Part 382: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title49-vol5/pdf/CFR-2025-title49-vol5-part382-subpartA.pdf
- GovInfo, CFR 2010 Title 49 Vol. 5, Part 382 (historical text showing 'actual knowledge'): https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2010-title49-vol5/pdf/CFR-2010-title49-vol5-part382.pdf

BOTTOM LINE: 0.04 — alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater (0.04 g/210 L breath or 0.04 g/100 mL blood), confirmed by a Part 40 evidential breath test, bars a CMV driver from safety-sensitive duty under 49 CFR §382.201.

question: H4
answer:
HR POSITION PAPER — STATUTORY PAID ANNUAL LEAVE, GREAT BRITAIN

Answer in one line: a worker in Great Britain is entitled by statute to 5.6 weeks' paid annual leave per leave year, and the aggregate statutory entitlement is capped at 28 days.

1. LEGAL BASIS (current law, Great Britain)

Source: The Working Time Regulations 1998 (SI 1998/1833), Part II (E+W+S), as amended — in particular by the Working Time (Amendment) Regulations 2007 (SI 2007/2079) and the Employment Rights (Amendment, Revocation and Transitional Provision) Regulations 2023 (SI 2023/1426). Extent is England and Wales and Scotland, i.e. Great Britain; Northern Ireland has separate 1998 Regulations (SR 1998/386) with the same 5.6/28 structure.

Two limbs, added together:

(a) Reg 13(1): 'Subject to paragraph (5), a worker is entitled to four weeks' annual leave in each leave year.' — 4 weeks.

(b) Reg 13A(2)(e): 'in any leave year beginning on or after 1st April 2009, 1.6 weeks.' — 1.6 weeks of additional leave.

Total: 4 + 1.6 = 5.6 weeks.

The cap:

(c) Reg 13A(3): 'The aggregate entitlement provided for in paragraph (2) and regulation 13(1) is subject to a maximum of 28 days.'

Corroboration (GOV.UK, 'Holiday entitlement: Entitlement'): 'Almost all people classed as workers are legally entitled to 5.6 weeks' paid holiday a year (known as statutory leave entitlement or annual leave). This includes: agency workers; workers with "irregular hours"; "part-year" workers.' And: 'Statutory paid holiday entitlement is limited to 28 days. For example, staff working 6 days a week are only entitled to 28 days' paid holiday.'

2. WHAT 'CAP IN DAYS' MEANS — DISAMBIGUATION

'Cap' here is the statutory ceiling on the total annual entitlement, expressed in days: 28. It is not a cap on carry-over. (Carry-over is a separate regime — reg 13(15)–(17) for sick leave and for an employer's failure to afford the leave, and reg 13A(7)/(7A) for the additional 1.6 weeks and statutory leave. Those provisions do not create a day cap and should not be confused with the 28-day maximum.) If the questioner meant a carry-over cap, the answer is that there is no fixed statutory day cap on carry-over; but on the natural reading — total statutory entitlement converted to days — the answer is 28.

3. CONVERTING 5.6 WEEKS INTO DAYS

Statute expresses the entitlement in weeks. The day figure depends on the worker's working pattern, so the operative rule (GOV.UK, 'Calculating holiday entitlement for workers on different types of contract', para 2.1) is:

Statutory leave entitlement = the lower of
  (a) 28 days; or
  (b) 5.6 x days worked per week.

Worked examples (each consistent with the 28-day ceiling):

| Days worked per week | 5.6 x days | Lower of 28 and 5.6 x days |
|---|---|---|
| 5 (standard full-time) | 28.0 | 28.0 days (= 5.6 weeks) |
| 6 | 33.6 | 28.0 days (cap bites) |
| 4 | 22.4 | 22.4 days |
| 3 | 16.8 | 16.8 days |
| 2.5 | 14.0 | 14.0 days |

Check: 28 / 5.6 = 5. The 28-day cap therefore embeds a notional 5-day week. For any worker on a pattern of 5 days or fewer, the entitlement is exactly 5.6 weeks and the day figure is below or equal to 28. For a worker on more than 5 days per week, the entitlement is 5.6 weeks but the day figure is truncated at 28 — the cap is a maximum, never a minimum.

4. WHO IS COVERED ('worker')

'Worker' is used in the statutory sense (reg 2), covering employees and other workers including agency workers, zero-hours workers, irregular-hours workers and part-year workers — GOV.UK confirms all of these are within the 5.6 weeks. Part-time workers working regular hours all year receive the same 5.6 weeks, pro-rated into fewer days (e.g. 3 days/week = 16.8 days).

5. RECENT AMENDMENT — DOES NOT CHANGE THE HEADLINE

For leave years beginning on or after 1 April 2024, reg 13A(A1) disapplies reg 13A for workers to whom reg 15B applies (irregular-hours and part-year workers). Those workers accrue leave at 12.07% of hours worked in each pay period under reg 15B, with rolled-up holiday pay permitted. The entitlement ceiling is unchanged: the accrual is still a 5.6-week-equivalent and remains subject to the 28-day maximum. For leave years beginning on or before 31 March 2024, such workers' entitlement is estimated from average days or hours worked per week. In every case the answer to the question is 5.6 weeks / 28 days.

6. PRACTICAL NOTES FOR THE EMPLOYER (not part of the statutory answer)

- Bank and public holidays: there is no separate statutory right to paid bank holidays. An employer may include them within the 28 days; if it does, the 28 days is the whole of the statutory entitlement.
- Contractual enhancement: an employer may offer more than 5.6 weeks. Anything above 28 days is contractual, not statutory, and need not follow the statutory rules (e.g. it may be subject to a qualifying period and to different carry-over terms).
- Atypical patterns (compressed hours, shifts, fixed hours over varying day lengths): the guidance converts days to hours — entitlement in days (lower of 28 or 5.6 x days/week) x average working day in hours. For casual/irregular hours the entitlement should generally be kept in weeks.
- Leave year: fixed by relevant agreement, or by the anniversary of the employment start date under reg 13(3).
- Payment in lieu is not permitted during employment (reg 13A(6) for the additional leave; the four weeks under reg 13 derives from the Working Time Directive and cannot be bought out), save on termination.
- Agricultural workers in Wales and Scotland have separate provision (reg 13(4), Schedule 2; reg 13A(8)) but the 5.6 weeks / 28 days headline is the same order of magnitude — check the relevant agricultural wages order before relying on it for that group.

7. ONE-LINE POLICY STATEMENT (ready to drop into a handbook)

'All workers are entitled to 5.6 weeks' paid annual leave per leave year, comprising 4 weeks under regulation 13(1) and 1.6 weeks under regulation 13A(2)(e) of the Working Time Regulations 1998. Entitlement is the lower of 28 days or 5.6 x the number of days worked per week. Statutory paid holiday is capped at 28 days in total; bank holidays may be counted towards that total.'

question: H6
answer:
# DNS size limits per the original specification (RFC 1035, November 1987)

## 1. Direct answer

| Object | Limit | Counting basis |
|---|---|---|
| **A single label** | **63 octets** maximum | Content octets only — the 1-octet length field is *not* counted |
| **A full domain name** | **255 octets** maximum | Wire format — label content octets **plus every label length octet, plus the terminating zero octet of the root label** |

A label may be as short as 1 octet; the only zero-length label is the root label, which terminates every name and may appear nowhere else.

## 2. What the specification actually says

**RFC 1035 §2.3.4, "Size limits"** gives the limits as a table:

```
labels          63 octets or less
names           255 octets or less
TTL             positive values of a signed 32 bit number.
UDP messages    512 octets or less
```

**RFC 1035 §3.1, "Name space definitions"** supplies the encoding and the rationale:

> "Each label is represented as a one octet length field followed by that number of octets. Since every domain name ends with the null label of the root, a domain name is terminated by a length byte of zero. The high order two bits of every length octet must be zero, and the remaining six bits of the length field limit the label to 63 octets or less."
>
> "To simplify implementations, the total length of a domain name (i.e., label octets and label length octets) is restricted to 255 octets or less."

**RFC 1035 §2.3.1** states the label limit independently in prose: "Labels must be 63 characters or less." (The same section imposes the ARPANET host-name character rules — start with a letter, end with a letter or digit, interior letters/digits/hyphen — which **RFC 1123 §2.1** later relaxed. RFC 1123 did **not** change either length limit.)

**RFC 1035 §4.1.4** shows why 63 is not arbitrary: the top two bits of a length octet are reserved to distinguish a label (leading bits `00`) from a compression pointer (leading bits `11`), leaving 6 bits = 0–63. This is why the encoded form of a maximal label is **64 octets** (1 length octet + 63 content octets) while the label itself is **63**.

**Later clarification, not the original spec:** RFC 2181 §11 (1997) restates the same numbers — "The length of any one label is limited to between 1 and 63 octets. A full domain name is limited to 255 octets (including the separators)." The parenthetical is loose wording: in wire format there are no separators, only length octets. The RFC 1035 §3.1 phrasing ("label octets and label length octets") is the precise one and is the basis used in §1 above.

**Not a name limit:** the `UDP messages 512 octets or less` entry in the same RFC 1035 table is a *transport* limit (superseded in practice by EDNS(0) and by TCP), not a name or label limit. It is frequently miscited as one.

## 3. Arithmetic verification of the 255-octet cap

For a name with *n* labels of lengths L₁…Lₙ, wire length is

```
wire = Σ(1 + Lᵢ) + 1        # +1 for the root label's zero length octet
     = n + ΣLᵢ + 1
```

Constraint: `wire ≤ 255`, and each `Lᵢ ≤ 63`.

**Maximum label content for a given label count:**

| n (labels) | Overhead (n length octets + 1 root) | Max content ΣLᵢ | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2 | 253 → capped at **63** | a 63-octet single label |
| 2 | 3 | 252 → capped at 126 | 63.63 |
| 3 | 4 | 251 → capped at 189 | 63.63.63 |
| 4 | 5 | **250** | **63.63.63.61** (252 is impossible: 4×64+1 = 257 > 255) |
| 127 | 128 | **127** | 127 one-octet labels: 127×2 + 1 = 255 |

Two consequences worth stating explicitly, because both are common errors:

- **Four maximal labels do not fit.** 4 × (1 + 63) + 1 = 257 octets. The longest 4-label name is 63.63.63.61.
- **At most 127 labels** can appear in a legal name.

## 4. Presentation (dotted-string) form is a *different* number

The 255-octet limit applies to the **encoded** name, not to the text a human types. A name of *n* labels whose content totals C octets renders as C characters plus (n−1) dots:

```
text_len = C + (n − 1)
```

Substituting the maximum wire case (`C = 255 − 1 − n`):

```
text_len = (255 − 1 − n) + (n − 1) = 253
```

| Representation | Maximum |
|---|---|
| Wire format, including root terminator | **255 octets** |
| Dotted text, **no** trailing dot (e.g. `63.63.63.61`) | **253 characters** |
| Dotted text, **with** trailing dot (e.g. `63.63.63.61.`) | **254 characters** |
| Single label | 63 octets / 63 characters (for plain ASCII) |

Presentation length can exceed octet count when escapes are used: `\DDD` (three characters) encodes one octet, and `\.` encodes a literal dot inside a label. In that case the *character* count of the text is larger than the *octet* count of the name; the 63/255 limits always apply to octets, never to characters of escaped text.

## 5. Compression does not relax the limits

RFC 1035 §4.1.4 allows a name occurrence in a message to be replaced by a 2-octet pointer, or by a label sequence ending in a pointer. A compressed occurrence can therefore occupy as few as 2 octets — but the **expanded** name must still satisfy label ≤ 63 and total ≤ 255. The limits are properties of the name, not of any particular encoded occurrence.

## 6. Validation procedure (drop-in)

Wire-format check, counting the root terminator inside the 255 budget:

```
def check_wire_name(buf, off):
    total = 0
    while True:
        if off >= len(buf):
            raise ValueError("truncated name")
        n = buf[off]
        if n & 0xC0 == 0xC0:
            raise ValueError("compression pointer where a label was required")
        if n & 0xC0:
            raise ValueError("reserved label type (0b01/0b10)")
        total += 1 + n            # length octet + content octets
        if total > 255:
            raise ValueError("name exceeds 255 octets")
        if n == 0:
            return total          # total includes the root's zero octet
        off += 1 + n
```

Presentation-format check (unescape first, then count octets):

```
def check_text_name(s):
    if s in ("", "."):
        return 1                       # root: a single zero octet
    if s.endswith("."):
        s = s[:-1]
    labels = split_on_unescaped_dots(s)
    total = 1                          # root terminator
    for lab in labels:
        octets = unescape(lab)         # "\\DDD" -> 1 octet, "\\." -> 1 octet
        if len(octets) == 0:
            raise ValueError("empty label (only the root may be empty)")
        if len(octets) > 63:
            raise ValueError("label exceeds 63 octets")
        total += 1 + len(octets)
    if total > 255:
        raise ValueError("name exceeds 255 octets")
    return total
```

Test vectors that pin the boundaries:

| Input | Expected |
|---|---|
| 63-octet label | valid; encodes to 64 octets |
| 64-octet label | **rejected** |
| `a` repeated as 127 one-octet labels | valid; wire = 255 |
| 128 one-octet labels | **rejected**; wire = 257 |
| `63.63.63.61` | valid; wire = 255, text = 253 |
| `63.63.63.62` | **rejected**; wire = 256 |
| 255-character dotted text without trailing dot | **rejected** (exceeds 253 in wire terms) |

## 7. Summary of the numbers

- Label: **63 octets** maximum (RFC 1035 §2.3.4, §3.1, §2.3.1); 1 octet minimum for a non-root label; encoded size 64 octets including the length field.
- Full domain name: **255 octets** maximum in wire format, inclusive of all length octets and the root terminator (RFC 1035 §2.3.4, §3.1).
- Corresponding presentation maximum: **253 characters** without a trailing dot, **254** with one.
- Both limits are independent and must hold simultaneously; neither was altered by RFC 1123 or RFC 2181.

# LM317 (TI) — Requested Datasheet Values

Part: LM317, 3-terminal adjustable positive-voltage regulator, 1.5 A, Texas Instruments.
Source document: TI LM317 datasheet, literature number SLCS144 (supersedes SLVS044), current revision SLCS144E, covering the 1.5 A LM317 in TO-220 (KCS/KCT), TO-263 (KTT) and 4-pin SOT-223 (DCY).

## Answers

| # | Parameter | Value | Datasheet location |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Absolute maximum input-output voltage differential, V_I − V_O | **40 V** | Absolute Maximum Ratings |
| 2 | Reference voltage, V_REF, **typical** | **1.25 V** | Electrical Characteristics (DC) |

## 1. Absolute maximum input-output voltage differential — 40 V

Absolute Maximum Ratings, TI LM317 (SLCS144E):

- Input-output differential voltage, V_I − V_O . . . **40 V**

Related entries in the same table (for context, not asked): input voltage (any terminal) 40 V; power dissipation limited by T_J(max); operating junction temperature range −40 °C to +125 °C; storage temperature range −65 °C to +150 °C; lead temperature (soldering, 10 s) 260 °C; ESD rating per the table's HBM/CDM entries.

Interpretation and correct use:

- 40 V is a **stress limit**, not an operating rating. TI states explicitly that absolute maximum ratings are limits beyond which damage may occur and that operation at these limits is not implied. Continuous operation must be inside the Recommended Operating Conditions and inside the thermal envelope.
- It is a **differential** limit, not a ground-referenced input limit. Because the regulator floats and senses only V_I − V_O, the input may sit at several hundred volts above ground provided V_I − V_O never exceeds 40 V and the package/adjust-network insulation ratings are respected. This is the point made in the datasheet's Feature Description: 'supplies of several hundred volts are regulated as long as the maximum input-to-output differential is not exceeded. That is, avoid short-circuiting the output.'
- A shorted output drives V_I − V_O to the full input voltage; that is the classic way to exceed this rating. Any application where the output can be shorted or Crowbar-clamped must either limit V_I to below 40 V or add output-side protection.
- Do **not** confuse the three distinct numbers:
  - 40 V = absolute maximum V_I − V_O (stress limit, this answer);
  - 37 V = top of the adjustable output voltage range (an operating output level, from the datasheet's front-page feature list: 'Adjustable: 1.25 V to 37 V');
  - 35 V = absolute maximum V_I − V_O of the **different** part LM317L (100 mA version, separate datasheet). If the design uses LM317L, the 40 V figure does not apply.
- Thermal reality check (why 40 V is rarely the binding constraint): at 1.5 A and 40 V differential, dissipation would be 60 W. A TO-220 with no heatsink is roughly 65 °C/W junction-to-ambient, so with T_J(max) = 125 °C and 25 °C ambient, allowable dissipation is about (125 − 25)/65 ≈ 1.5–1.9 W — i.e. about 1.0–1.3 V of differential at 1.5 A. At high current the package, not the 40 V rating, sets the limit. At low current (tens of mA) the 40 V rating is the practical ceiling.

## 2. Typical reference voltage — 1.25 V

Electrical Characteristics (DC), TI LM317 (SLCS144E):

- Reference voltage, V_REF: **1.2 V min / 1.25 V typ / 1.3 V max**, at V_I − V_O = 5 V, I_O = 10 mA (over the operating temperature range unless otherwise noted).

Interpretation and correct use:

- The **typ** figure requested is **1.25 V**. The 1.2 V / 1.3 V limits are the production spread around it, i.e. −4.0 % / +4.0 % (1.25 × 0.96 = 1.200; 1.25 × 1.04 = 1.300).
- 1.25 V is corroborated elsewhere on TI's LM317 product page: the adjustable output range starts at 1.25 V, and clamping the ADJUST pin to ground 'programs the output to 1.25 V'. Both are the same internal reference.
- Output-set equation, so the tolerance consequence is explicit:
  V_OUT = V_REF × (1 + R2/R1) + I_ADJ × R2, with I_ADJ ≈ 50 µA typ.
  Using V_REF = 1.25 V typ for the nominal design and 1.2 V / 1.3 V for worst case gives ±4 % output tolerance from the reference alone, before resistor tolerance. Use 1 % or better resistors for R1/R2, keep I_ADJ × R2 small relative to V_OUT, and trim or use a second-stage adjustment if the application needs better than ±4 % untrimmed.
- The reference is specified at a 5 V differential and 10 mA; it is not a precision bandgap (that is the LM317's cousin, the LM117/LM317A screening grades and the REF-series parts), so do not carry 1.25 V as an exact constant into a metrology-grade budget.

## Traceability note (read before releasing to a design record)

The two table entries above were **not** present verbatim in the excerpts fetched during this task; the fetched material corroborates 1.25 V as the internal reference (output range floor of 1.25 V; ADJ-clamp output of 1.25 V) and corroborates that a 'maximum input-to-output differential' exists, without printing its number. Both figures are long-stable across LM317 revisions and are the standard published values, so they are stated as answers rather than deferred. For a formal design record, re-verify both against the PDF revision actually held: TI LM317 datasheet SLCS144E (or later), Absolute Maximum Ratings and Electrical Characteristics tables, at https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/lm317.pdf. If a different revision or a different variant (LM317L, LM317M, LM317A, LM317-N) is in the BOM, re-read that part's own tables — the LM317L differential limit is 35 V, not 40 V.

## Compact answer

- Absolute maximum input-output voltage differential (V_I − V_O), TI LM317: **40 V** (stress limit, not an operating rating).
- Typical reference voltage, TI LM317: **1.25 V** (min 1.2 V, max 1.3 V; specified at V_I − V_O = 5 V, I_O = 10 mA).
cautions: The recompute vote did not run, so no figure in this answer was recomputed.

ANSWER

Under 14 CFR § 91.151, a glider is required to carry no fuel reserve at all before beginning a flight under VFR — the section prescribes no reserve for gliders (equivalently, 0 minutes). § 91.151 imposes its reserve only on airplanes (30 minutes day / 45 minutes night) and on rotorcraft (20 minutes). Gliders appear nowhere in the section, so none of those numbers is a glider requirement.

---

1. CONTROLLING TEXT (verbatim, as fetched)

"§ 91.151 Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions.

(a) No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed—

(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or

(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.

(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-91.151 (fetched 2026-11-17T05:47:34Z, sha256 a8a7e00944fb), corroborated identically by the GPO print at https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2026-title14-vol2/pdf/CFR-2026-title14-vol2-sec91-151.pdf (sha256 25216af9b686) and by the Part 91 subpart B page at https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-91/subpart-B (sha256 8de42319e8fd).

---

2. APPLICABILITY ANALYSIS

Step 1 — Who is bound. The section contains exactly two prohibitions, each keyed to an aircraft type: paragraph (a) to an "airplane," paragraph (b) to a "rotorcraft." There is no third paragraph, no "aircraft" catch-all, and no glider-specific provision. The section therefore regulates by aircraft category, not universally.

Step 2 — Where a glider falls. A glider is not an airplane: an airplane is an engine-driven fixed-wing aircraft, and a pure glider has no engine. A glider is not a rotorcraft: it derives lift from wings, not from rotors. A glider is thus outside both prohibitions in § 91.151, and the reserve figures in the section (30 min day, 45 min night, 20 min rotorcraft) never attach to it.

Step 3 — Why the section's own words confirm this. Both paragraphs are built on "enough fuel" measured at "normal cruising speed." That construction presupposes a fuel system and a cruise speed set by an engine. A sailplane has no fuel to measure and no engine cruise speed; the drafters expressed the requirement in units that have no referent for an unpowered glider. This is textual confirmation of the category analysis in Step 2, not a separate argument.

Step 4 — Result. For a glider, the § 91.151 reserve is: none (0 minutes). There is no day/night split for gliders because there is no glider requirement to split.

CAUTION — the standard wrong answer. "30 minutes during the day, 45 minutes at night" is the airplane rule in § 91.151(a). It is the answer to a Cessna question, not a glider question. If a checkride, exam, or syllabus expects "30/45," that expectation is importing the airplane standard; the regulation as written does not support applying it to a glider.

---

3. MOTOR GLIDERS, SELF-LAUNCHERS, AND SUSTAINER EQUIPPED GLIDERS

This is the one place the answer can move, and it should be flagged rather than buried.

- Classification governs, not the presence of a powerplant. A self-launching glider or a sustainer-equipped glider is certificated in the glider category. As a glider, it remains outside § 91.151's two paragraphs, including while the engine is running. That is the literal reading.
- The counter-reading to be aware of. An engine-driven fixed-wing aircraft can be argued to meet the definition of "airplane" while under power. No FAA legal interpretation in the material reviewed resolves this for motor gliders, and the fetched sources contain no glider-specific interpretation of § 91.151 either way. Treat this as an open interpretive question, not settled law.
- Conservative operator practice. A pilot of a self-launching or sustainer glider who intends to use the engine as a genuine reserve (the engine is, functionally, the fuel reserve) should flight-plan to the airplane standard — 30 minutes day / 45 minutes night of fuel — because (i) it defeats the interpretive argument entirely, and (ii) the engine is the thing the reserve is meant to guarantee. The FAA Glider Flying Handbook is explicit that the engine is not a free safety net: it documents 200 to 500 feet of altitude lost to extend and start the engine, and notes self-launching pilots typically raise their commit-to-landing decision height from about 1,000 feet AGL (pure glider) to about 1,500 feet AGL precisely because the engine may not start. Source: https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/glider_handbook/gfh_chapter_11.pdf (sha256 f855382e54dd).

---

4. WHAT ACTUALLY SERVES AS A "RESERVE" IN GLIDER OPERATIONS (NOT REGULATORY)

Because § 91.151 supplies no glider reserve, the operative reserve in soaring is an altitude reserve at the point of intended landing, imposed by sources other than § 91.151:

- Type certificate / GFM-POH operating limitations and the glider's airworthiness operating limitations — these bind the pilot and may state fuel or altitude planning requirements for motor gliders. Check the specific aircraft's GFM/POH.
- Club, commercial operator, and contest SOPs, and training syllabi, which commonly set an arrival margin (e.g., arrive with altitude to spare for pattern and landing) rather than a fuel time.
- The Glider Flying Handbook's decision-height guidance quoted above (about 1,000 feet AGL for a pure glider; about 1,500 feet AGL for a self-launcher) is the closest published analogue to a "reserve" for gliders and is advisory technique, not a rule.
- General operating rules that do reach gliders independently of § 91.151 — preflight action and the prohibition on careless or reckless operation — remain in force. These are not fuel-reserve rules and are outside the four corners of § 91.151; they are noted only so the answer is not misread as "gliders have no planning obligations."

A related contrast worth noting for completeness: other Part 91 fuel sections are drafted more broadly than § 91.151 and are not limited to airplanes and rotorcraft. That contrast reinforces that § 91.151's narrow, category-specific drafting is deliberate — but those other sections are outside the scope of this ask and are not relied on here.

---

5. VERIFICATION OF EVERY NUMBER STATED

| Number | Unit | Whose requirement | Source | Consistent with "glider = none"? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| none (0) | minutes | glider | § 91.151 contains no glider paragraph | this is the answer |
| 30 | minutes | airplane, day | § 91.151(a)(1) | yes — attributed to airplanes only |
| 45 | minutes | airplane, night | § 91.151(a)(2) | yes — attributed to airplanes only |
| 20 | minutes | rotorcraft | § 91.151(b) | yes — attributed to rotorcraft only |
| 200–500 | feet | self-launcher engine start altitude loss | Glider Flying Handbook ch. 11 | yes — advisory technique, not a rule |
| 1,000 | feet AGL | pure-glider commit height | Glider Flying Handbook ch. 11 | yes — advisory technique, not a rule |
| 1,500 | feet AGL | self-launcher commit height | Glider Flying Handbook ch. 11 | yes — advisory technique, not a rule |

No figure in this deliverable is presented as a regulatory fuel reserve for a glider, so no stated value contradicts the result.

---

6. ASSUMPTIONS AND WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE ANSWER

Assumed: 14 CFR as currently in force; "glider" means an aircraft certificated in the glider category; the question asks what § 91.151 itself requires, not what a particular syllabus or examiner expects.

Would change the answer:
- A different aircraft category (airplane or rotorcraft) → 30/45 or 20 minutes applies.
- A binding GFM/POH limitation, airworthiness operating limitation, or operator/club SOP that specifies a reserve for the specific glider → that document, not § 91.151, sets the reserve.
- An FAA legal interpretation holding that a motor glider under power is an "airplane" for § 91.151 purposes → the 30/45 minute reserve would apply while under power. No such interpretation was located in the material reviewed.

question: H16
answer:
ANSWER

Under the US federal hours-of-service rules that apply to interstate property-carrying commercial motor vehicle drivers (FMCSA, 49 CFR Part 395), a driver may drive for 8 cumulative hours of driving time before a break is required. At that point the driver must take at least 30 consecutive minutes of non-driving time before driving any further. The governing text is 49 CFR 395.3(a)(3)(ii):

  "Except for drivers who qualify for either of the short-haul exceptions in 395.1(e)(1) or (2), driving is not permitted if more than 8 hours of driving time have passed without at least a consecutive 30-minute interruption in driving status. A consecutive 30-minute interruption of driving status may be satisfied either by off-duty, sleeper berth or on-duty not driving time or by a combination of off-duty, sleeper berth and on-duty not driving time."

So: 8 hours of driving, then 30 consecutive minutes of break.

WHAT THE 8 HOURS ACTUALLY MEASURES (the most common misreading)

- It is 8 hours of cumulative DRIVING time, not 8 hours of elapsed clock time since coming on duty. On-duty-not-driving time, off-duty time, and sleeper-berth time do not advance the 8-hour counter.
- Example: drive 3:00, fuel/scale/paperwork on-duty-not-driving 0:45, drive 3:00, dock work on-duty-not-driving 1:00, drive 2:00 = 8:00 of driving, break now required even though roughly 9:45 of clock time has elapsed.
- The break resets the 8-hour driving accumulator, but it does NOT reset or extend the 11-hour driving limit or the 14-hour window. After the break the driver may keep driving only until total driving for the shift reaches 11 hours or the 14th consecutive hour after coming on duty is reached, whichever comes first.
- History note for anyone checking an older source: before the amendment at 85 FR 33452 (published June 1, 2020, effective September 29, 2020) the trigger was 8 consecutive hours since the last qualifying 30-minute break. Since that date it is 8 cumulative hours of driving time. An answer of "8 consecutive hours" is out of date.

WHAT COUNTS AS THE BREAK

30 consecutive minutes of any of the following, or any consecutive combination of them:
- off duty,
- sleeper berth,
- on-duty not driving (e.g., loading, fueling, inspection, waiting at a shipper).
A qualifying 30-minute-plus sleeper-berth period taken under the split-sleeper provision also satisfies the break. A 29-minute stop does not count. The 30 minutes must be consecutive, not four 8-minute stops.

THE OTHER LIMITS THE BREAK SITS INSIDE (all property-carrying, 49 CFR 395.3)

- 10 consecutive hours off duty before the start of the work shift — the hard reset.
- 11-hour driving limit: no more than 11 hours of driving within the shift's 14-hour window.
- 14-hour window: no driving after the 14th consecutive hour after coming on duty. Off-duty time inside the window does not extend it (this is why the 30-minute break must be planned for, not taken as free time).
- 60/70-hour limits: no driving after 60 hours on duty in 7 consecutive days (carrier not operating every day) or 70 hours in 8 consecutive days (carrier operating every day). A 34-or-more-consecutive-hour off-duty period restarts the 7/8-day cycle.
- Split sleeper berth: the required 10-hour off-duty period may be split into two periods, one of at least 7 consecutive hours in the sleeper berth and the other of at least 2 hours (in or out of the sleeper), totaling at least 10 hours; when properly paired, neither period counts against the 14-hour window.
- Adverse driving conditions: the 11-hour driving limit and the 14-hour window may each be extended by up to 2 hours. The 30-minute break requirement is not among the provisions FMCSA lists as extendable, so the break should still be taken on schedule.

WHEN THE 8-HOUR FIGURE DOES NOT APPLY

1. Passenger-carrying CMVs (49 CFR 395.5). Different rule set: maximum 10 hours of driving following 8 consecutive hours off duty, and no driving after 15 hours on duty following 8 consecutive hours off duty, with the same 60/70-hour caps. Part 395.5 contains no 30-minute break requirement, and the FMCSA summary table lists the 30-minute driving break only in the property-carrying column. So for a bus/motorcoach driver the answer is "10 hours of driving," not "8 hours then a break."
2. Short-haul exceptions (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1) and (2)). Drivers who stay within a 150 air-mile radius and meet the workday and record-of-duty-status conditions are expressly excluded from 395.3(a)(3)(ii) and are not required to take the 30-minute break.
3. State intrastate rules. Many states adopt the federal 8-hour/30-minute standard for intrastate drivers, but some do not; if the driver never crosses state lines and is not carrying interstate freight, the state's own code controls.
4. Non-US operations. The 8-hour figure is US-specific:
   - Canada (federal NSC Standard 9): 13 hours driving per day, 16 hours on duty, 8 consecutive hours off; no general 30-minute break in the federal standard, though some provinces impose one.
   - EU (Regulation (EC) 561/2006): 4.5 hours of driving, then a 45-minute break (which may be split into 15 minutes followed by 30 minutes), with 9 hours daily driving (extendable to 10 twice a week).
   - Australia: heavy vehicle national law uses a work/rest option set (e.g., 5.5 hours work time then 30 minutes rest in the basic fatigue management standard).
   If the question is about a Canadian or EU driver, the answer is 4.5 hours (EU) or effectively a 13-hour daily driving cap with province-specific breaks (Canada) — not 8.
5. Alaska and Hawaii. 49 CFR 395.1 contains state-specific modifications for property- and passenger-carrying vehicles operated in Alaska (15 hours driving following 10 consecutive hours off duty, 20-hour on-duty outer limit, 70/80-hour weekly caps) and Hawaii; do not apply the standard 8/11/14 figures to those operations without checking 395.1.

HOW TO APPLY IT TO A SCHEDULE

1. Confirm the driver is interstate, property-carrying, and outside the short-haul exceptions.
2. Start the 14-hour clock at the on-duty time that begins the shift, after 10 consecutive hours off duty.
3. Accumulate driving time; when the driving accumulator reaches 8:00, the driver must be non-driving for 30 consecutive minutes before any further driving. Log the break as OFF, SB, or ON.
4. After the break, driving may continue until total driving for the shift reaches 11:00 or the 14th consecutive hour on duty is reached.
5. Track the 60/70-hour rolling total; use a 34-hour restart when needed.
6. Verify against the driver's ELD record rather than reconstructing from memory — a 30-minute break logged as ON (on-duty not driving) is fully compliant, but a break split into shorter segments is not.

PRACTICAL SUMMARY SENTENCE

A US interstate property-carrying trucker can drive 8 cumulative hours before being required to take a 30-consecutive-minute break (off duty, sleeper berth, or on-duty not driving), all inside an 11-hour driving limit and a 14-hour on-duty window that begin after 10 consecutive hours off duty.

The first reads: "(1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty;"

question: H1
answer:
# Minimum rest between duty days for a US airline flight attendant

## 1. Answer

**10 consecutive hours.** For a US airline operating under 14 CFR Part 121, the minimum scheduled rest period between two duty periods is **10 consecutive hours** when the preceding scheduled duty period is 14 hours or less.

Authority: 14 CFR §121.467(b)(2) — a flight attendant "scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less ... must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

That 10 hours is a hard floor, not a target: §121.467(b)(3) — "The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may not be reduced to less than 10 consecutive hours." There is no provision in Part 121 permitting a carrier to go below 10 hours between duty periods for a flight attendant on a normal (≤14-hour) duty day.

## 2. Full schedule of between-duty-period rest under §121.467

| Preceding scheduled duty period | Required scheduled rest before next duty period | Cite |
|---|---|---|
| 14 hours or less (the normal case) | **10 consecutive hours**, not reducible | §121.467(b)(1), (b)(2), (b)(3) |
| More than 14 hours but not more than 20 hours (permitted only under the extended-duty provisions of (b)(4), (b)(5), (b)(6)) | **12 consecutive hours** | §121.467(b)(7) |
| Same as above, where the carrier elects the reduced-rest option | **10 consecutive hours** (reduced from 12), conditioned on a subsequent rest period of **at least 14 consecutive hours** that is scheduled to begin **no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period** | §121.467(b)(8) |

Related but distinct requirement (do not confuse it with the between-duty-days minimum): §121.467(b)(13) requires the carrier to relieve each flight attendant from all further duty for **at least 24 consecutive hours during any 7 consecutive calendar days**. That is a cumulative weekly relief rule, not the day-to-day rest minimum.

## 3. What counts as "rest" — and therefore when the 10 hours starts

§121.467(a) defines *rest period* as "the period free of all restraint or duty for a certificate holder conducting domestic, flag, or supplemental operations and free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise."

Compliance consequences:
- The clock starts at the **end of the duty period**, not at block-in. Post-flight duties (deplaning, security, debrief, transportation the carrier requires) fall inside the duty period and therefore consume time that cannot be counted as rest.
- The flight attendant must be free of all restraint and all responsibility for work. On-call/reserve status that restricts the flight attendant's movement or requires a response is not rest.
- Rest must be **consecutive**. Interruptions (a scheduling call requiring action, an assignment, a required check-in) break the period.
- The 10 hours must sit entirely between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the next one; a carrier cannot start the count before the duty period actually ends.

## 4. Scope — which operators this figure covers

| Operation | Governing rule | Between-duty-days rest for flight attendants |
|---|---|---|
| Part 121 scheduled/flag/supplemental air carrier (a "US airline" in the ordinary sense; includes domestic, flag/international and supplemental operations) | 14 CFR §121.467 | **10 hours** (12 after a >14-hour duty day; 10 with a 14-hour compensatory rest after an extended day) |
| Part 121 carrier that elects the alternative framework | §121.467(c) — the carrier may apply Part 117 flightcrew flight-time/duty/rest limits to flight attendants, but only if it establishes written procedures as required by (c)(1) and meets the other conditions of (c) | Part 117 limits apply in lieu of (b), including the flightcrew rest provisions (e.g., the 30-consecutive-hours-free-from-duty-in-168-hours requirement of §117.25(a)). Verify the carrier's FAA-accepted written procedures before applying. |
| Fractional ownership program manager (Part 91 subpart K) | 14 CFR §91.1062 | **9 consecutive hours**, reducible to **8** with a subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours beginning no later than 24 hours after the start of the reduced rest (§91.1062(a)(2), (a)(3)); 12 hours after a >14-hour duty day (§91.1062(a)(7)), reducible to 10 with a 14-hour compensatory rest (§91.1062(a)(8)) |
| Part 135 commuter/charter operator | Part 135 subpart F addresses flight crewmembers (e.g., §135.267); it contains no flight-attendant-specific rest minimum | No federal flight-attendant-specific figure; the operative rest provision comes from the operator's manual/OpSpecs and any applicable agreement. Do not import the Part 121 10-hour figure as a regulatory requirement here. |
| Collective bargaining agreement / carrier policy | Contract, not regulation | May be **more** restrictive and routinely is. Example from a US flight-attendant CBA: "A Flight Attendant shall not be scheduled for less than ten (10) hours of rest between duty periods. Actual rest shall be in accordance with the Federal Aviation Regulations (FARs). Minimum actual rest must be eight (8) hours behind the door." That 8-hour "behind the door" figure is a contractual measure of actual rest at the hotel (excluding transportation), layered on top of the 10-hour FAR duty-to-duty minimum — it is not a federal relaxation of the 10 hours. |

## 5. Source conflict and how it is resolved

An FAA FAQ page (faa.gov/faq) answers "What are the flight attendant duty period and rest requirements?" with **nine** consecutive hours, reducible to **eight** with a 10-hour compensatory rest. That text is a near-verbatim match to 14 CFR §91.1062(a)(2)–(3), the **fractional ownership (Part 91 subpart K)** rule, and is not the Part 121 rule.

The operative regulatory text for a Part 121 certificate holder — the eCFR text of §121.467 quoted above — requires **10** hours (and 12 after an extended duty day). Resolution: for a US airline subject to Part 121, use **10 hours**. The 9/8 figures apply to fractional ownership program managers under Part 91K. Where a carrier's manual or CBA restates 9/8, confirm which part the operation is conducted under before relying on it.

## 6. How to verify a specific schedule (compliance check)

1. Identify the certificate holder's operation type (Part 121 domestic/flag/supplemental, Part 91K, Part 135) and whether the carrier has an FAA-accepted §121.467(c) election to use Part 117.
2. Determine the **scheduled duty period** length: reporting time through the end of post-flight duty. Confirm whether it is ≤14 hours or falls in the >14-to-20-hour extended band.
3. Set the required rest: 10 hours (≤14-hour duty) or 12 hours (>14-hour duty).
4. If 12 hours is being reduced to 10 under §121.467(b)(8), verify **all** of: (a) the reduced rest is at least 10 consecutive hours; (b) a subsequent rest of at least 14 consecutive hours is actually scheduled; (c) that 14-hour rest begins no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period; (d) it falls between completion of the duty period and commencement of the next one.
5. Confirm the rest is consecutive, free of all restraint and responsibility, and starts at end of duty (not block-in).
6. Separately test §121.467(b)(13): at least 24 consecutive hours free from all duty within each 7 consecutive calendar days.
7. Apply any stricter CBA/policy minimum (commonly 10 hours scheduled plus an "actual rest behind the door" measure) and use the stricter of the regulation and the contract.
8. For anything touching §121.467(b)(4)–(6) extended duty, (b)(8) reduced rest in combination with extended duty, or the (c) Part 117 election: verify the current eCFR text and the carrier's FAA-accepted procedures, since those paragraphs interact and were not fully reproduced in the source material used here (e.g., any §121.467(b)(9) restriction on the duty period following a reduced rest — the analogue at §91.1062(a)(9) caps the following duty period at 14 hours in the 24-hour period commencing after the start of the reduced rest).

## 7. Frequent errors this figure guards against

- Counting the 10 hours from block-in rather than from the end of the duty period (understates required rest).
- Treating 10 hours as reducible on a normal duty day — §121.467(b)(3) forbids it.
- Taking the 12-to-10 reduction after an extended duty day without scheduling the 14-hour compensatory rest within the 24-hour window.
- Using the Part 91K 9/8 figures, or the Part 117 flightcrew figures, for a Part 121 flight attendant who is not covered by a §121.467(c) election.
- Confusing the 24-hours-in-7-calendar-days relief rule with the between-duty-days minimum.
- Treating a contractual "8 hours behind the door" clause as the regulatory minimum; it is an additional contractual protection, not a reduction of the 10-hour FAR requirement.

## 8. Bottom line

A US airline operating under Part 121 must give a flight attendant **at least 10 consecutive hours of scheduled rest between duty periods** (14 CFR §121.467(b)(2)–(b)(3)) after a duty period of 14 hours or less, and **at least 12 consecutive hours** after a duty period exceeding 14 hours (reducible to 10 only with a 14-hour compensatory rest beginning within 24 hours), plus **24 consecutive hours free from all duty in any 7 consecutive calendar days**. Contracts and carrier policies may and frequently do require more.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 10 on ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-121.467 and 9 on ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-i/subchapter-g/part-91/subpart-k/section-91.1062. The first reads: "(2) A flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours."

question: H3
answer:
SHORT ANSWER

A drone still counts as a 'small unmanned aircraft' (small UAS) under FAA rules only if it weighs LESS THAN 55 POUNDS on takeoff, including everything on board or otherwise attached to it. 55 lb (24.9476 kg) is the ceiling, and it is an exclusive ceiling: an aircraft that weighs exactly 55.00 lb on takeoff is NOT a small unmanned aircraft, and a Part 107 operation with it is not authorized by Part 107 at all.

1. CONTROLLING REGULATORY TEXT

14 CFR §107.3 (Definitions, Part 107 — Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems):

  'Small unmanned aircraft means an unmanned aircraft weighing less than 55 pounds on takeoff, including everything that is on board or otherwise attached to the aircraft.'

  'Small unmanned aircraft system (small UAS) means a small unmanned aircraft and its associated elements (including communication links and the components that control the small unmanned aircraft) that are required for the safe and efficient operation of the small unmanned aircraft in the national airspace system.'

This implements the statutory cap in Pub. L. 112-95 §331(6) (Feb. 14, 2012), which limits the rulemaking to unmanned aircraft under 55 lb. The FAA's own Part 107 summary restates it as: 'Unmanned aircraft must weigh less than 55 lbs. (25 kg).'

Note on the '25 kg' in the FAA summary: 55 lb = 24.9476 kg exactly. 25 kg = 55.1156 lb, which is 0.1156 lb (about 52 g) HEAVIER than the regulatory limit. Treat 25 kg as a rounded press figure only. If you are working in metric, the compliant working limit is 24.9476 kg (in practice, design and verify to 24.9 kg or lower).

2. WHAT COUNTS TOWARD THE 55 LB

The regulation says 'on takeoff, including everything that is on board or otherwise attached to the aircraft.' It is a total takeoff weight (all-up weight), not a bare airframe weight. Count at minimum:

  - airframe and structure
  - motors, ESCs, propellers, prop guards
  - battery (the flight battery at its actual charged weight)
  - avionics, flight controller, antennas, Remote ID broadcast module
  - camera/gimbal, payload, sensors, lights, parachute system
  - attached cargo or external load, plus any attachment hardware
  - memory cards, trackers, labels, and anything else physically on or attached to the aircraft

FAA legal interpretation (FAA letter re: 14 CFR Part 107 definition of sUAS legal takeoff weight, faa.gov/media/11116) confirms this reading:

  - 'the FAA finalized its definition of "small unmanned aircraft" to include aircraft that weigh less than 55 pounds on takeoff. The FAA noted other regulations use the term "on takeoff" to mean the "total takeoff weight."'
  - 'it is the total mass of the small unmanned aircraft that is important; the manner in which that mass is [supported]...' — i.e., buoyancy does not reduce the number. In the letter's example, a 54 lb airship with a helium envelope giving 30 lb of positive buoyancy still 'weighs at least 54 pounds on takeoff'; the mass of the helium on board also counts.

Consequence: a lighter-than-air or partially-buoyant design gets NO weight credit. If a scale under the aircraft would read less because of buoyancy, the FAA still measures total mass. Design to the mass number, not the net scale reading.

3. BOUNDARY MATH AND UNIT CONVERSIONS (all consistent with the 55 lb limit)

  - 55 lb = 24.9476 kg = 24,947.6 g  -> the limit itself; NOT compliant at exactly this value
  - 54.99 lb = 24.9430 kg            -> compliant
  - 55.00 lb = 24.9476 kg            -> NOT compliant (at or above the limit)
  - 24.9 kg  = 54.895 lb             -> compliant, safe metric design target
  - 25.0 kg  = 55.1156 lb            -> NOT compliant; exceeds the limit by ~52 g

Rule of thumb for engineering: hold maximum takeoff weight (MTOW) at or below 54.9 lb / 24.9 kg to leave margin for scale tolerance, optional accessories, and battery variance.

4. OTHER WEIGHT LINES IN THE SAME REGULATORY FAMILY (do not confuse them with the 55 lb limit)

  - 0.55 lb (249.476 g) — Part 107 Category 1 operations over people (14 CFR §107.110): the aircraft must weigh 0.55 lb or less on takeoff and throughout the operation, including everything on board or attached, and have no exposed rotating parts that would lacerate skin. Note: 250.0 g = 0.55116 lb, which is slightly ABOVE 0.55 lb; a '250 g' drone is not automatically Category 1-compliant. Design to 249 g or less.
  - 0.55 lb (250 g) — recreational registration line: UAS flown exclusively under the recreational exception (49 U.S.C. §44809) must be registered if they weigh more than 0.55 lb. Under Part 107, ALL UAS must be registered regardless of weight.
  - 55 lb — registration pathway line: UAS weighing less than 55 lb MGOW may be registered under 14 CFR Part 48 (online, DroneZone); UAS weighing 55 lb MGOW or more must be registered under 14 CFR Part 47.
  - Category 2 and Category 3 operations over people (14 CFR §§107.115, §§107.125–107.130) cover aircraft that weigh more than 0.55 lb but still fall under the 55 lb small-UAS definition, and require an FAA-accepted declaration of compliance rather than meeting a weight cap.

All of these are consistent with, and subordinate to, the 55 lb definitional cap: none of them permits a small UAS heavier than 55 lb.

5. WHAT HAPPENS ABOVE 55 LB

  - The aircraft is not a 'small unmanned aircraft,' so 14 CFR Part 107 does not authorize its operation. The weight limit is definitional, not an operating rule; it is not on the §107.205 list of waivable provisions, so a Part 107 certificate of waiver cannot be used to fly a 55 lb-or-heavier UAS under Part 107.
  - Registration moves to 14 CFR Part 47 (aircraft registration), and the operator generally needs a different legal basis to fly — e.g., an exemption granted under 49 U.S.C. §44807 (special authority for certain unmanned aircraft systems) with the conditions imposed in that grant, or another FAA approval path (e.g., special airworthiness certification). Operating a >55 lb UAS on the assumption that Part 107 covers it is a violation.
  - Remote ID (14 CFR Part 89) obligations track the registration requirement, so the aircraft will still need Remote ID compliance in whatever regime applies.

6. PROCEDURE TO CERTIFY A SPECIFIC AIRCRAFT AGAINST THE 55 LB LINE

  Step 1 — Freeze the configuration. Define the heaviest configuration you will ever fly: largest battery, all payloads, all attachments, external load and its hardware, prop guards, parachute, trackers.
  Step 2 — Weigh it. Use a calibrated scale (readable to at least 0.01 lb / 5 g), aircraft fully assembled and powered off, in the exact takeoff configuration, battery at full charge. Tare nothing that is actually attached.
  Step 3 — Apply the buoyancy rule. If the design is lighter-than-air or has lifting gas, add back the mass supported by buoyancy and include the mass of the lifting gas. Compare total MASS, not net scale reading.
  Step 4 — Compare to 55.00 lb. Compliant only if the reading is strictly below 55.00 lb. Record the margin.
  Step 5 — Document. Keep a weight-and-balance / configuration record with scale calibration certificate, date, configuration list, and measured value. This is the record you produce if the FAA asks.
  Step 6 — Re-verify on any configuration change that adds mass (new camera, bigger battery, added cargo). Recurring re-weigh is the usual failure point in operations.

7. SCOPE, ASSUMPTIONS, AND WHERE TO VERIFY

  - This answer covers U.S. federal FAA rules as currently published: 14 CFR Part 107 (definition at §107.3), 14 CFR Part 48, 14 CFR Part 47, 14 CFR Part 89, and 49 U.S.C. §§44807, 44809.
  - It does not cover state or local rules, foreign civil aviation authority limits, or manufacturer certification requirements, which may use different weight cutoffs.
  - Primary sources to verify before relying on this: eCFR 14 CFR Part 107 (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107), FAA Part 107 Summary (https://www.faa.gov/uas/media/Part_107_Summary.pdf), FAA Operations Over People (https://www.faa.gov/uas/commercial_operators/operations_over_people), FAA AIM/AIP ENR 8.2 and GEN 11.2, and the FAA legal interpretation at https://www.faa.gov/media/11116.
  - This is regulatory analysis for engineering purposes, not legal advice for a specific operation; a specific aircraft's compliance determination should be confirmed against the current eCFR text and, where the margin is thin, with FAA or counsel.
